# Qdrant ES Gateway

> Elasticsearch-compatible application search backed by Qdrant. Compatibility is intentionally scoped.

## Start here


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/compatibility.md

# compatibility

# Compatibility and semantic differences

Supported requests cover CRUD, mappings, bulk ingestion, common index lifecycle calls, multi-search, cursor pagination, basic lexical search, payload filters, source projection, count, complete filter-only aggregations, health, and durable aliases. Request bodies must be valid UTF-8; malformed byte sequences are rejected before JSON or NDJSON parsing instead of being stored as Unicode replacement characters. Index creation enforces the static name rules shared by Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9: lowercase UTF-8 names of at most 255 bytes, excluding their reserved punctuation, the leading `_`/`-`/`+` forms, and the exact names `.` and `..`. Invalid names return HTTP 400 with `invalid_index_name_exception` before catalogue or Qdrant work. Dot-prefixed names other than `.` and `..` remain accepted; the gateway does not emulate engine-specific deprecation warnings, hidden-index settings, or system-index ownership. Creating an index that already exists returns HTTP 400 with `resource_already_exists_exception` before Qdrant work; it does not replace the stored mapping. Names that collide only after Qdrant collection normalization remain a distinct gateway validation error. `PUT /<index>/_mapping` merges new non-text properties into the existing mapping and creates Qdrant payload indexes for supported filterable types; identical existing definitions are idempotent, while type changes and new text fields are rejected. New text fields require a new index because the pinned Qdrant 1.15 schema cannot add their named sparse vectors to an existing collection. Both `POST` and `PUT` bulk requests are accepted. Bulk `update` and `delete` actions require an explicit `_id`; every action line must name exactly one supported action with object metadata and string `_index`/`_id` values. Malformed actions fail before any item is executed instead of assigning an unrelated generated ID or partially applying the request. Standalone and bulk `index` operations check the authoritative document store so a new document returns HTTP 201 with `result: "created"`, while replacing an existing document returns HTTP 200 with `result: "updated"`. Qdrant 1.15.5 reports an absent single point as HTTP 404 rather than a successful null result; that specific response is treated as a missing document, while a missing collection remains an upstream 502. Document HEAD requests preserve the same distinction: an absent point is 404, but transport and storage failures are 502 rather than false “not found” results. HEAD responses are bodyless and include the Elasticsearch product header. Contiguous bulk index writes remain one Qdrant upsert batch and use one batched existence lookup rather than a read per item. Successful bulk `create`, `update`, and `delete` items preserve the operation's result metadata and report the concrete backing index when addressed through an alias. Standalone and bulk `create` operations first check for an existing document and return a 409 conflict rather than overwriting it; they are serialized within one gateway process but are not an atomic cross-replica compare-and-insert. Index existence checks likewise describe the preflight state rather than providing atomic compare-and-write semantics. The compatibility analyzer at `GET /_qdrant_gateway/compatibility` is local-only and reports request counts; no telemetry leaves the process.

Search requests with `size: 0` are accepted for aggregation-only use and return no hits; the gateway uses a one-item internal scroll because Qdrant rejects a zero scroll limit. `from` and `size` must be non-negative integers, `size` cannot exceed `MAX_PAGE_SIZE`, and their combined result window cannot exceed 10,000. Cursor requests require an array with one scalar value per explicit sort field and cannot combine `search_after` with a non-zero `from`. Invalid pagination fails before index lookup or Qdrant access rather than silently using defaults or truncating the page. Native filter-only searches issue an exact Qdrant count alongside the bounded hit retrieval, so `hits.total` is not truncated to `from + size`. Ranked text searches derive lower-bound totals from their candidate window. Filter-only post-filter searches and complete gateway scans compute totals over all matching pages; concurrent writes can change what a scan observes. Boolean and non-negative integer `track_total_hits` modes follow the OpenSearch/Elasticsearch response shape: `false` omits `hits.total` and skips the otherwise eligible exact-count request, while a numeric threshold caps the reported value and changes the relation to `gte` when the threshold is exceeded. Numeric thresholds currently shape the response but do not terminate Qdrant's exact count early. The `_search` and `_msearch` endpoints also honor OpenSearch's `rest_total_hits_as_int=true` query parameter: ordinary totals become integers and disabled totals use the native `-1` sentinel. Lowercase `true` and `false` are accepted; as in OpenSearch 3.9.0, an empty or valueless parameter enables the mode. Other values and the native-incompatible combination of integer formatting with a numeric tracking threshold fail before Qdrant work. Integer formatting cannot express the gateway's usual `eq`/`gte` accuracy relation for bounded text searches. Strict `track_total_hits` parsing intentionally excludes OpenSearch's undocumented coercion of strings, fractional numbers, and negative values. The extra count can add an upstream round trip to filter-only search latency. Supported filter-only aggregations scan every matching Qdrant page independently of the returned hit count. Ranked text and pattern queries with aggregations fail explicitly.

Search `_source` filtering accepts booleans, a single field pattern, an array of patterns, or an `include`/`includes` and `exclude`/`excludes` object. Dotted paths and `*`/`?` wildcards preserve the nested object shape rather than flattening selected fields, and the same parser is used for collapse inner hits. Invalid types, mixed-type arrays, and unknown options fail before index lookup or Qdrant work. Filtering shapes the response after the gateway has hydrated each candidate's complete source; it reduces returned data but does not reduce source-read bandwidth or memory use.

Partial `doc` updates use read-merge-write semantics. Inner objects are merged recursively; arrays and scalar values replace the existing value. Identical merged documents return `result: "noop"` without an upstream write by default; `detect_noop: false` forces the write. A missing document can be created explicitly with either `doc_as_upsert: true` or a separate `upsert` object; the separate form writes the `upsert` source rather than the partial `doc`, while an existing document still receives `doc`. Both standalone and bulk update paths share this behavior. In the default embedded-source mode, non-text updates refresh the complete stored `_source` and all mapped filter/sort payload fields in one payload write; this preserves untouched source fields and keeps filtering consistent with document reads. This path transfers the merged source even when the patch is small. Updates are not an atomic compare-and-write, Elasticsearch `nested` query semantics remain unsupported, scripts remain unsupported, and version counters remain approximate.

Aliases currently map one alias to one concrete index. CRUD, search, count, mapping, and multi-search requests resolve that concrete index before selecting a Qdrant collection or deriving a deterministic point ID. Alias inspection is Elasticsearch-shaped and keyed by the concrete index. Alias action batches are fully validated before a single SQLite transaction applies them, so a malformed later action cannot leave an earlier routing change behind. Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 both preserve the original target when an `add` action attaches the same alias to a second index. Because the gateway cannot represent that multi-index state, it rejects such a final topology before changing the catalogue instead of silently replacing the original target. An atomic batch that removes the old target and adds the new one remains supported in either action order. Native alias filters, routing fields, write-index/hidden flags, remove `must_exist`, and unknown action options are rejected before catalogue access instead of being acknowledged and discarded. Multi-index aliases, filtered aliases, write-index selection, routing, hidden aliases, and Qdrant-native alias switching remain unsupported.

Qdrant's server-side BM25 uses sparse vectors and its own tokenization/model implementation. Results should be evaluated by relevant document IDs and product metrics, not numerical `_score` equality with Elasticsearch. `match_phrase` currently uses the same native lexical representation and is therefore not a Lucene positional phrase guarantee.

Filter-only `should` clauses and numeric or percentage `minimum_should_match` are supported when they can be represented as Qdrant filter alternatives. Scalar and array forms of `must_not` are accepted, and nested filter-only bools preserve their clause boundaries when negated or used as alternatives. As in Elasticsearch, a `bool` containing `must` or `filter` defaults `minimum_should_match` to zero; without either required clause, at least one `should` remains required. Optional filter-only clauses preserve the matching document set but do not boost Qdrant scores. `dis_max`, `match_bool_prefix`, and fuzzy-shaped requests are accepted through the gateway's lexical field path; their ranking and typo/prefix semantics are intentionally approximate because Qdrant's sparse model is not Lucene. Basic response sorting accepts a field name, a direct order such as `{"price":"asc"}`, or the standard options object `{"price":{"order":"desc"}}`; `_score` defaults to descending and other fields default to ascending. Unsupported sort options and invalid directions are rejected instead of silently changing the order. Filter-only field sorting and `search_after` visit every matching page and retain the best `from + size` hits, so point order cannot hide a later winner. Ranked text searches still sort a bounded candidate window. Cursors do not freeze the data: use stable data and a unique explicit tie-breaker for repeatable pages. Scripts, scroll, and analyzer settings that would materially change semantics remain unsupported. Every rejection identifies the request feature and a safe alternative where one exists.

Field collapse accepts one field and one standard `inner_hits` definition with `name`, `size`, `_source`, and `_id` in `fields`. The response uses the requested inner-hit name, caps its size at `MAX_PAGE_SIZE`, and applies its source projection independently of the top-level projection. Unsupported collapse options, multiple inner-hit definitions, and inner-hit sorting are rejected before Qdrant work. Collapse follows the candidate scope of its query; complete filter scans retain all group members, so collapse memory is proportional to matching documents. Collapse with `search_after` is rejected. Ranked text collapse remains limited to retrieved candidates.

`exists` queries over mapped payload fields exclude missing values, JSON `null`, empty arrays, and arrays containing only `null`; empty strings and arrays with at least one non-null value count as present. This matches the ordinary Elasticsearch boundary, but not mapping-dependent cases such as `index: false`, `ignore_above`, or malformed values ignored by an analyzer. Server-side `exists` filtering is limited to fields mirrored into the searchable Qdrant payload; `post_filter` evaluates the hydrated `_source`.

For application mappings that expose a conventional `.keyword` multi-field name, exact filters, range and exists predicates, gateway-side patterns, sorting, collapse, and terms facets resolve that suffix to the base payload/source field. This makes client-generated requests such as `term: {"brand.keyword":"Acme"}` consistent across native and hydrated-source paths. It does not create a second analyzed representation or emulate custom multi-field analyzers: the base field must still be suitable for the requested operation.
# Pattern queries

`regexp`, `prefix`, and `wildcard` clauses are evaluated by the gateway using Rust's regular-expression engine after candidate documents are read from Qdrant. Positive pattern clauses can be combined with ordinary Qdrant-translated filters in `bool.must` or `bool.filter`; pattern clauses in `should` and `must_not` are rejected rather than approximated. Pattern-only search and count requests scan the collection in bounded scroll pages, so their totals are exact for the stable collection snapshot seen by the scan, but they are useful only for modest catalog and identifier searches and should not be used as a substitute for a dedicated indexed pattern field at very large scale. Wildcards preserve the position of Elasticsearch/OpenSearch-style `*` and `?` operators, including leading, trailing, and consecutive stars. Gateway-side matching uses stored source strings, so prefix and wildcard case behavior on analyzed `text` fields can differ from a native engine's normalized term dictionary; use a normalized keyword field when case behavior is part of the contract. Regular expressions use Rust/RE2-style syntax and reject invalid expressions with a structured 400 response.

Search responses also accept `post_filter` for simple term, terms, numeric range, exists, match-all, and bool clauses. The complete `post_filter` tree is validated before index lookup or Qdrant work; unsupported query types, unknown bool options, ambiguous multi-field clauses, and malformed range options return a structured 400 instead of silently producing an empty result set. The filter is applied to hydrated hits after the main query. Min, max, terms, filter, keyed filters, and supported calendar histograms reduce every query-matched page before hit-only post-filtering, collapse, or cursor selection. Scalar and array-valued source fields use the same any-element matching rule for term, terms, range, prefix, wildcard, and regexp predicates, keeping gateway-side evaluation aligned with native Qdrant filters. Arrays of objects still require Elasticsearch `nested` semantics and are unsupported. Aggregation memory uses constant metric state and at most 10,000 distinct buckets per aggregation, with at most 100 aggregations per request. Exceeding a bound fails instead of returning partial results. Calendar histograms accept day, week, month, and year intervals, IANA timezones, and explicit `min_doc_count: 1`; unsupported formats, bounds, offsets, and empty-bucket filling fail. Timezone rules come from the compiled chrono-tz dependency. Scans are not point-in-time snapshots. In document-projection mode, aggregation fields must be supported mapped payload fields; reductions use search-projection values. See the [comparison fixture](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/validation/aggregations).

### Explicit sparse embeddings

New indices can map a top-level field as `sparse_vector`. Optional
`method: {name: seismic, engine: lucene}` is accepted for OpenSearch request
compatibility; Qdrant performs exact sparse dot-product search, not SEISMIC.
The optional engine may be omitted. Other method keys, the native engine and
pruning options are rejected. Named vectors are provisioned at index creation;
adding sparse fields through `_mapping` requires a new index.

Documents supply a token-weight object, for example `{"v":{"65536":1.0}}`.
Keys must be canonical decimal unsigned 32-bit IDs; weights must remain positive
and finite after float32 conversion. IDs are never hashed, folded or narrowed.
Missing/null fields omit the vector; an empty document vector is allowed.
Malformed vectors fail before any source or search write in that write batch.
Bulk index operations isolate invalid sparse documents as per-item 400 errors,
allowing adjacent valid items to proceed. Partial updates rebuild sparse vectors
when the sparse field changes, including with document projection enabled.

`{"query":{"neural_sparse":{"v":{"query_tokens":{"65536":1.0}}}}}`
supports one mapped field as the sole top-level query. Inference (`query_text`,
`model_id`), `method_parameters`, bool composition, sort, search_after, collapse,
post_filter, min_score and aggregations are rejected. `from`/`size` retain gateway limits;
reported total hits are a lower bound. Query token objects must not be empty. Scalar predicates (including exists, term,
range and nested bool filters), filter/metric aggregations on sparse fields or
their token subpaths are rejected for search and count; sparse vectors are not
scalar payload fields.
The OpenSearch Lucene default-path comparison in `examples/explicit-sparse`
verifies full-width token IDs; it does not reproduce SEISMIC approximation bugs.

## Shared metadata and consistency

SQLite remains the default single-replica catalog. The optional [Redis/Valkey catalog](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/shared-catalog.md) shares mappings and single-index aliases across replicas, with explicit recovery after uncertain administrative writes. It does not supply atomic document updates or snapshot pagination. Unsupported `pit` search bodies and URL parameters `if_seq_no`, `if_primary_term`, `version`, `version_type`, `retry_on_conflict`, `op_type`, `routing`, and `scroll` return a structured 400 rather than being ignored.

### Ordered numeric searches

Single-field numeric sorts can use Qdrant's ordered scroll when every matching
point carries a gateway-generated scalar-type marker. This avoids downloading
all matching documents to return one page. Multiple sort fields, missing or
array values, integers outside the exact floating-point comparison range,
separate document projections, and ties crossing the requested page boundary
retain the complete scan. The `search_after` predicate excludes the cursor value;
exact totals still describe all query matches before pagination.

New writes carry versioned eligibility metadata in the reserved
`_qeg_fast_fields` payload field. New collections and mapping updates index that
field; old points without markers safely use the existing scan. Application
mappings cannot define this reserved field. No reindex is required for correctness.
Neither ordered scroll nor the fallback is a point-in-time snapshot during
concurrent writes. Qdrant's [ordered-scroll API](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/points/#order-points-by-payload-key)
provides the backend ordering; the gateway checks compatibility before using it.

Exact keyword `terms` and simple keyword `term` / numeric `range` filter
aggregations can also use Qdrant facet/count indexes after checking the matching
payloads' eligibility markers. Facets request exact counts and up to 10,001
values, preserving the existing 10,000-bucket error and `sum_other_doc_count`.
Other reducers and unsafe or legacy values retain streaming evaluation.
The [facet API](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/payload/#facet-counts)
counts each distinct value once per document, including multivalued keywords.

An older mapping that already owns `_qeg_fast_fields` is treated as user data:
its values and index type are preserved, and fast paths are disabled for that
index. New mappings cannot introduce that name. These optimizations add no
cursor sessions, result cache, or Redis/Valkey dependency.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/architecture.md

# architecture

# Architecture

The gateway is a small Axum service with three boundaries:

```text
Elasticsearch client / REST
          |
   compatibility handlers
          |
 translation + response shaping
          |
      Qdrant REST API
          |
      Qdrant collections
```

Each ES index maps to a Qdrant collection named `es_<safe-index-name>`. SQLite stores mappings, vector names, and aliases in the default single-gateway deployment. The optional [Redis/Valkey catalog](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/shared-catalog.md) keeps authoritative metadata outside the gateway; each request materializes a fresh ephemeral SQLite view. Gateway replicas then require no durable local catalog. Metadata administration uses an explicit ownership/recovery protocol; there is no transaction spanning the catalog and Qdrant. Documents are payload-first: the original source is stored under `_source`, while mapped non-text fields are mirrored for Qdrant filtering, sorting, and aggregations.

When `DOCUMENT_PROJECTION=true`, every index also has `es_<safe-index-name>_documents`. This second collection is a durable document projection with no payload indexes and no HNSW graph. Qdrant 1.15 requires a vector field on points, so the gateway uses a one-dimensional on-disk placeholder vector and `m=0`; it is never searched. The searchable collection contains sparse representations plus only `_es_id`, `_es_index`, and mapped non-text fields. GETs and search response hydration read the authoritative `_source` from the document collection in a batch, which avoids storing the full source in the searchable collection. A full write persists the document projection first, then updates the searchable projection. `ASYNC_SEARCH_PROJECTION=true` uses Qdrant's asynchronous operation acknowledgement for the second step, so metadata-only writes can be acknowledged without waiting for sparse-index maintenance. The gateway itself owns no document queue or source cache.

Synchronous point writes and payload-index creation send Qdrant's `wait=true` URL parameter, so acknowledgment waits for the operation to finish. Asynchronous modes send `wait=false`. Earlier gateway revisions placed this control in the JSON body, which did not enforce completion; historical ingestion timings from those revisions measure acknowledgment rather than guaranteed completed writes. Completion is distinct from a transaction across collections or a guarantee about every replica's read visibility.

The two collections are intentionally not treated as one transaction. The source write is the durability boundary; projection updates must be idempotent and should be retried/reconciled by an external durable worker in an HA deployment. Filter and sort fields that must be read-after-write correct must remain mirrored in the searchable collection. Unmapped metadata can remain source-only. This is an explicit eventual-consistency mode, not an attempt to hide the trade-off behind local state.

Text fields get named sparse representations populated using Qdrant's server-side `qdrant/bm25` Document model. `multi_match` queries each requested field and merges unique hits with the declared boost. This is intentionally a useful application-search approximation, not Lucene score identity.

Point IDs are UUID-shaped values derived from SHA-256(index, NUL, ES ID). The original ID remains in `_es_id`; GET/update/delete therefore remain deterministic across restarts.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/production.md

# production

# Production deployment guide

The gateway is designed to be a stateless HTTP tier for document and search state held in Qdrant. It does not provide authentication, authorization, TLS termination, or Elasticsearch cluster semantics; place it behind an ingress/API gateway and restrict network access to the Qdrant endpoint.

## Container

Images are published to `ghcr.io/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway` for version tags. The image runs as UID 10001, has no Linux capabilities, and uses a read-only root filesystem in the Helm chart. Persist `/data` when using the default SQLite catalog. Shared-catalog deployments instead require durable Redis/Valkey storage; see [shared catalog operation and recovery](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/shared-catalog.md).

Use immutable version tags or image digests in production:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway:0.1.0
```

Every release workflow produces a multi-architecture image, BuildKit provenance, an SPDX SBOM, a cosign SBOM attestation, and Trivy vulnerability results. The release job fails on known fixed HIGH or CRITICAL image vulnerabilities; unfixed findings are retained in the scan results for review.

The gateway applies a 5-second Qdrant connection timeout and a 180-second upstream request timeout by default. Set `QDRANT_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` and `QDRANT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` to change them. When `ASYNC_PAYLOAD_WRITES=true`, `ASYNC_WRITE_QUEUE` bounds detached writes (256 by default); a full queue returns an upstream error instead of allowing background tasks to grow without limit.

The SQLite metadata connection uses a five-second busy timeout and `synchronous=FULL`. This helps with short local lock contention, but it does not make a shared network filesystem safe for multiple gateway replicas.

After the first release, open the repository's Packages settings and change the GHCR package visibility to Public if GitHub created it privately. Link the package to this repository and enable Dependabot alerts, security updates, and secret scanning in repository Security settings.

## Kubernetes

The chart is in `deploy/helm/qdrant-es-gateway`. Qdrant is intentionally external so its clustering, replication, backups, and storage lifecycle can be managed independently.

```bash
helm upgrade --install search-gateway deploy/helm/qdrant-es-gateway \
  --set image.tag=0.1.0 \
  --set qdrant.url=https://qdrant.example.internal:6334 \
  --set qdrant.existingSecret=qdrant-credentials
```

Before exposing the service:

1. Configure ingress TLS and client authentication.
2. Create a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy allowing egress only to Qdrant and DNS.
3. Set resource requests and limits from workload measurements.
4. Keep the default SQLite deployment at one replica. For multiple replicas, configure the optional shared catalog, initialize or migrate it deliberately, and follow its durability and recovery requirements. Do not share SQLite files over a network filesystem.
5. Configure Qdrant replication, snapshots, monitoring, and disk alerts independently.
6. Enable `DOCUMENT_PROJECTION=true` and `ASYNC_SEARCH_PROJECTION=true` only with a durable reconciliation process for projection lag or failed asynchronous operations.

## Operational checks

- `/healthz` is a liveness check.
- `/readyz` checks Qdrant connectivity and should gate traffic.
- `GET /` exposes the compatibility/version response.
- Watch Qdrant segment growth, optimizer backlog, disk utilization, search latency, and projection lag.
- Keep request and bulk limits bounded; request bodies are buffered in memory, and each concurrent `POST /_bulk` or `POST /<index>/_bulk` may consume up to `MAX_BULK_BYTES` before parsing. Do not expose the service directly to the public internet.
- Test the actual mappings and unsupported-query behavior before migration.

## Release process

1. Bump the package version in `Cargo.toml` and the chart version in `deploy/helm/qdrant-es-gateway/Chart.yaml`.
2. Merge the tested change to `main`.
3. The release workflow creates the matching `vX.Y.Z` tag, publishes the multi-architecture GHCR image, packages the Helm chart, and creates the GitHub release. If that version tag already exists, the workflow skips publishing.
4. Review the GitHub Actions image scan and SBOM attestation.
5. Promote the immutable image digest through environments.

Use the manually triggered `Release dry run` workflow to validate version metadata, build the image, scan it, and package the chart without creating a tag, logging into GHCR, or publishing anything.

The repository's CI does not publish private voice, video-generation, or local development artifacts.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/migration.md

# migration

# Migration guide

1. Create a representative index and mapping through the normal ES API.
2. Re-ingest documents with `_bulk` or use Qdrant's official migration tooling for the data-movement portion.
3. Point the existing Elasticsearch client at the gateway URL.
4. Run representative traffic and inspect `/_qdrant_gateway/compatibility`.
5. Compare matching IDs, filter correctness, p95 latency, and relevance labels against Elasticsearch.

Do not migrate a workload that depends on Kibana, observability APIs, scripts, nested/parent-child semantics, or arbitrary aggregations without redesigning those paths.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/application-validation.md

# application-validation

# Real-application validation targets

The validation strategy is endpoint-only: run one application workflow twice and change only its Elasticsearch-compatible base URL. This proves both that the application needs no gateway-specific client code and that returned documents are usable by the application.

## First target: Spinscale catalogue search

[Spinscale's ecommerce search app](https://github.com/spinscale/elasticsearch-ecommerce-search-app) is the best first published application target. It exercises index mappings, bulk ingestion, full-text product search, filters, sorting, pagination, facets, and source-bearing hits. Its original build is tied to an older Java/Gradle/Micronaut stack, so the practical validation path is to preserve its request shapes and fixture data in a modern, pinned replay harness before attempting a full application upgrade.

The current gateway can validate the basic catalogue slice directly. The remaining gaps before claiming unchanged full-application compatibility are custom analyzers/synonyms, exact fuzzy and prefix ranking, search-scoped aggregation membership, and the complete Elasticsearch bulk response contract. `post_filter`, basic metric/filter aggregations, `dis_max`, fuzzy-shaped requests, and retail-style `more_like_this` plus `collapse`/`inner_hits` response shapes are now accepted, but their semantics remain explicitly approximate where the underlying Qdrant query is not Lucene-equivalent.

## Second target: AWS Retail Demo Store search

[AWS Retail Demo Store](https://github.com/aws-samples/retail-demo-store) has a useful isolated search service, although the full storefront is AWS-heavy and uses OpenSearch. Its search API returns product IDs and then retrieves product details separately. The request shapes include typeahead `match_bool_prefix`, `dis_max`, category diversity through `collapse`/`inner_hits`, and “similar products” via `more_like_this`. The gateway now accepts these shapes, so the next step is live request replay and product-quality comparison; exact prefix ranking, category distribution, and similarity relevance still need validation before a no-code application claim.

The smallest credible sequence is:

1. run the repository's `validation/replay.py` against native Elasticsearch and the gateway;
2. add a pinned Spinscale request fixture and compare its top-k IDs, sources, filters, facets, and pagination;
3. run the AWS search container locally and capture its real HTTP requests;
4. replay those requests against both endpoints, measuring result equivalence separately from ranking quality.

The current request-level audit is maintained in [demo-app-compatibility.md](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/demo-app-compatibility.md). It separates transport/response compatibility from semantic equivalence so “the application can make the request” is not confused with “the two engines rank and aggregate identically.”

The endpoint replay has also been run against native OpenSearch 3.6.0. The [2026-10-09 field note](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/2026/10/09/opensearch-wildcards-keep-the-leading-star.html) records 10 of 12 application checks passing after correcting leading-wildcard translation, with analyzed-text prefix case behavior and bounded-window cursor ordering retained as explicit differences. The official `opensearch-py` 3.2.0 client separately completed the supported CRUD/search workflow against the gateway; this verifies client transport behavior, not full server parity.

Do not compare raw `_score` values. Compare exact sources for the same IDs where ordering is not the product contract, and use top-k overlap, nDCG, zero-result rate, facet equality, and pagination continuity for ranked results.

## Performance protocol

Use identical payloads, IDs, refresh policy, warm-up, concurrency, and client connection settings for both endpoints. Record bulk time, update latency, search p50/p95/p99, mixed-workload throughput, error rate, CPU, memory, disk, and freshness. Run the lightweight fixture first, then 50,000 and 500,000 document corpora. Keep compatibility assertions and performance measurements as separate report sections so a faster but semantically different result cannot be mistaken for a successful application validation.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/benchmarking.md

# benchmarking

# Benchmarking

The reproducible comparative benchmark is `benchmark/run.sh`. It starts native Elasticsearch, Qdrant, the Rust gateway, and a containerized Python client on one Docker host. A large profile loads 500,000 synthetic products in batches of 5,000, measures updates and full-source reads, then runs a mixed workload of searches, reads, updates, and deletes at concurrency 50. Compose limits the services to approximately four CPUs and fifteen GB of memory, while `ES_HEAP` explicitly controls the Elasticsearch JVM heap for a comparable memory profile.

```bash
cd benchmark
DOCS=50000 BATCH=500 ./run.sh
```

Results are written to `benchmark/results/benchmark.json` and `benchmark/results/resources.txt`. Re-run with the same corpus, image versions, warm-up behaviour, and host profile when comparing changes.

For a real product corpus, see the external-dataset workflow in [`benchmark/README.md`](https://dstockton.github.io/benchmark/README.md). It downloads the public H&M catalogue, converts selected product fields to JSONL, mounts that generated file read-only into the runner, and executes the same benchmark client against both endpoints.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/contributing.md

# contributing

# Contributing

Install Rust, Docker, and run `make test` and `make lint`. Integration tests require Docker and a reachable Qdrant. Keep unsupported behavior explicit: do not silently discard an ES clause. Add a unit test for each new translator rule and an integration fixture for each Qdrant API dependency.

After changing an article or the compatibility, architecture, production, or migration guide, run `python3 scripts/export_agent_docs.py`. Commit the generated `docs/markdown/`, `docs/llms.txt`, and `docs/llms-full.txt` alongside the source changes. CI checks that they remain synchronized. Markdown exports have no front matter, so Jekyll copies them as literal text files.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/demo-app-compatibility.md

# demo-app-compatibility

# Demo-application compatibility

This page records request-level compatibility against the two public application targets that motivated the gateway work. “Supported” means that the gateway accepts the request shape and returns the fields the application consumes. It does not mean Lucene-identical ranking, analyzer behavior, or refresh/version semantics.

## AWS Retail Demo Store search service

The isolated search service in [aws-samples/retail-demo-store](https://github.com/aws-samples/retail-demo-store) uses an OpenSearch-compatible client and sends:

| Request feature | Gateway status | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| `match_bool_prefix` across several fields | ✅ | Accepted through the gateway lexical path; typo/prefix ranking is approximate |
| `dis_max` with boosts and tie breaker | ✅ | Query shape accepted; Qdrant scoring is not Lucene/OpenSearch scoring |
| `collapse` on `category.keyword` | ✅ | Gateway-side grouping after retrieval |
| `inner_hits` with `_source: false` and `_id` consumption | ✅ | The standard named definition returns `category_hits`, grouped totals, bounded hits, and independent source suppression |
| `more_like_this` by document ID | ✅ | Expanded into a gateway lexical query using the referenced source |
| `from`/`size` | ✅ | Bounded pagination |

The service's two search routes—product search and similar products—are therefore request-compatible with the gateway's supported subset. The remaining validation work is result-quality comparison on the demo corpus: category diversity, top-k overlap, and similar-product relevance must be measured rather than inferred from HTTP compatibility.

## Spinscale Elasticsearch e-commerce search app

The [spinscale/elasticsearch-ecommerce-search-app](https://github.com/spinscale/elasticsearch-ecommerce-search-app) exercises a broader catalogue workflow:

| Request feature | Gateway status | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| index existence, create, delete | ✅ | Durable gateway metadata and Qdrant collections |
| close/open/settings bootstrap calls | ⚠️ | Common request shapes are acknowledged; Elasticsearch analyzer/settings effects are not emulated |
| bulk indexing with immediate refresh policy | ✅ | Bulk response and refresh endpoint are supported; Qdrant is continuously available |
| `multi_match` with fuzziness and `minimum_should_match` | ⚠️ | Accepted lexical path; ranking and exact minimum-term semantics are approximate |
| `post_filter` | ⚠️ | Simple term/terms/range/exists/bool shapes are applied to hydrated hits |
| terms, min/max, filters aggregations | ⚠️ | Supported shapes are bounded by the gateway's candidate/facet implementation |
| source-bearing hits, updates, deletes, counts | ✅ | Covered by `validation/replay.py` |

The AWS target is the closest current fit for a no-client-change search path. The Spinscale target is a useful compatibility and relevance test, but it depends more heavily on Elasticsearch-specific analysis and aggregation semantics. The project should not claim 100% semantic replacement for either application until the real application workflows have been replayed and their product-level assertions pass.

## Additional application targets

These are worthwhile next targets because they are well-known open-source applications with documented Elasticsearch integrations. They are intentionally listed as targets, not as compatibility claims:

| Application | Elasticsearch role | Likely gateway fit | What a real replay must prove |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Zammad](https://github.com/zammad/zammad) | Ticket, user, organisation, knowledge-base and global search; Elasticsearch is enabled by default in the documented deployment configuration | Medium for simple text/filter/search flows; low for a drop-in replacement until Zammad's index schema and query builder are replayed | Search result IDs, field projections, pagination, sorting, counts, reindex lifecycle and freshness |
| [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab) | Optional advanced/global/code search across projects, work items, merge requests and other content | Low for the complete product; potentially useful for an isolated application-search slice, not GitLab's code-search workload | Exact search modes, permissions, aggregations, aliases, refresh behaviour and the multi-index schema |
| [Adobe Commerce / Magento Open Source](https://github.com/magento/magento2) | Required catalog search engine in current 2.4.x deployments; product search, filters, sorting and catalog indexing | Medium for a bounded catalogue-only test; low for the full adapter without analyzers, facets and Magento-specific mappings | Catalog reindex, searchable attributes, layered navigation facets, price/range filters, sort order, store scope and product visibility |
| [Open edX `edx-search`](https://github.com/openedx/edx-search) | Pluggable search backend; Elasticsearch is a supported legacy backend for LMS search | Medium for document indexing/search APIs; not a claim about the full Open edX platform | Document type filtering, field filters, pagination, exact result objects and update/delete freshness |

The first three applications use Elasticsearch as part of a larger product rather than exposing a simple public search API. That makes them valuable semantic tests, but permissions, analyzers, aliases, aggregations and refresh semantics can dominate the result.

## Public corpus benchmark targets

The reproducible benchmark now accepts an external JSONL corpus and includes an importer for the [Qdrant H&M product catalogue](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Qdrant/hm_ecommerce_products). It contains 105,126 product records in the downloaded snapshot and is published under CC BY 4.0. The corpus is downloaded and generated locally; it is not committed to this repository. The benchmark command and importer are documented in [benchmarking.md](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/benchmarking.md).

[Open Food Facts](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openfoodfacts/product-database) is a second useful scale target: its food split is millions of products and is available under the Open Database License. It is too large for routine CI and requires attribution/share-alike handling, so it should be run as an explicitly provisioned benchmark rather than bundled into the repository.

## Reproducible validation

Run the deterministic endpoint-only replay against native Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and the gateway:

```sh
python3 validation/replay.py \
  --native http://localhost:19200 \
  --gateway http://localhost:9200 \
  --output validation/results/latest.json
```

The replay now covers lifecycle calls, bulk ingestion, filters, facets, pattern queries, `_msearch`, cursor pagination, reads, updates, deletes, and counts. Compare IDs, sources, facet keys, and pagination behavior; do not compare raw engine scores.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/external-corpus-results.md

# external-corpus-results

# External corpus results

This is a reproducible snapshot, not a capacity promise. It records the first external-corpus comparison so later gateway changes can be checked against a real catalogue rather than only the synthetic fixture.

## H&M product catalogue

Source: [Qdrant's `hm_ecommerce_products` dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Qdrant/hm_ecommerce_products), 105,126 product records in the downloaded parquet snapshot, published under CC BY 4.0. The repository stores only the importer and benchmark instructions; the parquet and generated JSONL remain local and are not redistributed here.

The benchmark ran native Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and the Rust gateway backed by the Qdrant engine 1.15.3 in Docker Desktop, with the repository's approximate 1.5 CPU / 8 GB Elasticsearch, 1 CPU / 4 GB Qdrant, 1 CPU / 2 GB gateway and 0.5 CPU / 1 GB runner limits. It used identical JSONL batches and client code; only the ES-compatible endpoint changed. The query was a title match for `dress`, with 1,000 updates and 500 mixed requests at concurrency 10.

| Profile | Native Elasticsearch | Qdrant gateway | Gateway relative result |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Bulk ingest, `refresh=` disabled | 5.69 s | 10.14 s | 1.78x slower |
| Bulk ingest, `refresh=wait_for` per batch | 215.45 s (two-repeat median) | 2.90 s | Refresh semantics dominate this comparison |
| Search p95, concurrency 1 | 17.99 ms | 0.99 ms | 18.2x lower latency |
| Search p95, concurrency 10 | 82.40 ms | 3.54 ms | 23.3x lower latency |
| Mixed throughput, 500 requests | 740 req/s | 1,255 req/s | 1.70x higher throughput |
| 1,000 updates | 3.14 s | 1.82 s | 1.72x faster |

The refresh-wait profile is useful because it reflects an application that explicitly requests immediate visibility after every bulk batch. It must not be described as raw Elasticsearch indexing capacity: the no-refresh run shows native Elasticsearch completing the same corpus faster than the gateway. Conversely, the gateway's bulk path does not reproduce Elasticsearch refresh scheduling because Qdrant remains continuously queryable.

## Result quality

Both engines returned ten source-bearing hits for the same query. The top-ten IDs did not match exactly. That is expected from the current gateway's Qdrant sparse ranking versus Elasticsearch/Lucene analysis and scoring, but it is a material compatibility result: the gateway is currently a strong transport and performance candidate for application-search workloads, not a claim of 100% relevance equivalence. Future reports should add recall@k / overlap, category coverage and an application-specific judged relevance set.

The run also captured peak container memory: Elasticsearch 1.45 GiB, Qdrant 411 MiB and gateway 13 MiB at the sampling point. Disk measurements were unavailable from the host-side collector on Docker Desktop because its Linux VM volume paths are not exposed; run the same profile on Linux or collect the mounted paths from inside the containers before publishing storage comparisons.

## Reproduce

See [`benchmark/README.md`](https://dstockton.github.io/benchmark/README.md) for the download, attribution, conversion and benchmark commands. Run both profiles when comparing a client that requests immediate visibility and a client that allows refresh to be decoupled from bulk ingestion.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/internals.md

# internals

# Internals

The current implementation uses direct Qdrant REST calls to keep the protocol boundary visible and easy to audit. The metadata store is SQLite because it is durable, embedded, and small enough for index/mapping/alias metadata. It is not a document store.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/read-write-crossover.md

# read-write-crossover

# Read/write crossover

For product search, updates do not all need to block the user-facing request. A price or stock update can be accepted, applied asynchronously, and become searchable shortly afterwards. That makes the useful question less binary than “can the gateway beat a native write?”: how much of the workload is customer-facing retrieval, and how much is synchronous mutation?

## Focused mix sweep

The sweep used the same Elasticsearch-shaped client calls against both services:

- 50,000 product documents
- 1,000 requests per point
- 50 concurrent clients
- read/search traffic split evenly between `_search` and `GET _doc`
- write traffic made up of single-document `_update` calls
- `ASYNC_PAYLOAD_WRITES=true` for the gateway

| Read/search share | Write/update share | Elasticsearch throughput | Qdrant gateway throughput | Approximate winner |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 20% | 80% | 1,166.90 req/s | 962.31 req/s | Elasticsearch |
| 40% | 60% | 1,080.77 req/s | 1,177.88 req/s | Qdrant gateway |
| 60% | 40% | 1,071.20 req/s | 1,059.19 req/s | Near tie |
| 80% | 20% | 1,091.95 req/s | 1,308.47 req/s | Qdrant gateway |

The practical crossover is therefore around 40–60% read/search traffic for this profile. At roughly 40% reads, the gateway begins to lead on throughput; at 60%, the two paths are effectively tied; and at 80%, the gateway has a clear throughput advantage. This is a workload boundary, not a universal constant: corpus size, query shape, update fields, concurrency, and the freshness window all move it.

The 500,000-document mixed run reinforces the shape of the result. With 70% search/read and 30% update/delete traffic, throughput was 77.42 req/s for Elasticsearch and 263.32 req/s for the gateway. Search p95 was 4,213.6 ms versus 305.82 ms. The gateway’s asynchronous update mode is a good fit when the product can tolerate eventual search visibility for ordinary catalog changes.

![Bubble chart comparing corpus size, search p95 latency, and throughput](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/throughput-latency-corpus-bubbles.png)

## How to use the crossover

For a catalog workload dominated by imports, synchronous writes, or strict read-after-write requirements, native Elasticsearch remains the safer baseline. For a product experience dominated by retrieval—especially when updates can flow through an event queue or tolerate a short freshness delay—the gateway becomes increasingly attractive.

The next production decision should be based on the application’s freshness contract: measure the acceptable update-to-search delay, then place the workload on this curve using the same query mix and concurrency as the real service.

## Additional corpus scaling points

To make the bubble chart less dependent on the two original points, the same mixed workload was repeated at four smaller corpus sizes. These runs used the current gateway build, 50 concurrent clients, 1,000 mixed requests, and the existing 70% read/search versus 30% update/delete composition.

| Corpus | Elasticsearch throughput | Qdrant gateway throughput | Elasticsearch mixed search p95 | Qdrant gateway mixed search p95 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 10,000 | 749.48 req/s | 1,192.41 req/s | 125.06 ms | 97.10 ms |
| 25,000 | 982.57 req/s | 1,011.40 req/s | 101.34 ms | 97.23 ms |
| 50,000 | 1,037.89 req/s | 1,010.64 req/s | 96.90 ms | 101.20 ms |
| 100,000 | 935.91 req/s | 986.74 req/s | 103.94 ms | 102.97 ms |
| 500,000 | 77.42 req/s | 263.32 req/s | 4,213.60 ms | 305.82 ms |

The 10k–100k points were collected in the local four-CPU container profile. The 500k point is the previously captured production-shaped run, so it is useful for scale context but should not be treated as a perfectly controlled continuation of the smaller points. That distinction is called out directly in the chart.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/relevance.md

# relevance

# Relevance evaluation

Use a labelled query/corpus fixture and compare top-k IDs with Elasticsearch. Track MRR or NDCG, not raw score equality. Differences can come from analyzers, tokenization, field fusion, document length normalization, and BM25 implementation. A production migration should include domain-labelled queries before making an economics decision.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/shared-catalog.md

# Shared metadata across gateway replicas

The default SQLite catalog is still the simplest choice for one gateway. No measurement has established SQLite as a bottleneck. The optional Redis/Valkey catalog addresses **metadata ownership across replicas**, not faster search.

Set `CATALOG_REDIS_URL` to a `redis://` or TLS `rediss://` URL. All replicas serving the same Qdrant collections must use the same `CATALOG_REDIS_KEY` (default `qeg:{catalog}:v1`) and collection-related configuration. The URL may contain credentials; supply it through a secret. Redis Cluster is not a supported connection topology.

The authoritative catalog contains mappings, named vector metadata, and single-index aliases. Every request loads the current committed snapshot into an ephemeral SQLite database. There is no replica metadata cache and no persistent local metadata dependency in shared mode. Snapshot size is limited to 8 MiB. Index creation and mapping changes check the exact prospective serialized size before mutating Qdrant; alias batches check it before committing local metadata. Oversized changes return a validation error and release the administrative claim. Fetching and materializing the whole catalog on each request favors small catalogs and correctness; it is not a high-throughput optimization. Network operations time out after five seconds.

## Starting a new deployment

Use a dedicated durable Redis/Valkey instance, disable eviction, enable AOF persistence and select the durability/HA policy appropriate to your deployment. An acknowledged metadata update is only as durable as that server's configuration. Losing an acknowledged catalog update during asynchronous failover can invalidate ownership guarantees: do not automatically fail over to a stale replica and resume writes. Stop gateways, restore/reconcile the catalog and Qdrant, then restart. Redis/Valkey is an authoritative database here, not a disposable cache.

1. Start Redis/Valkey with `--appendonly yes --appendfsync always --maxmemory-policy noeviction` and a persistent volume.
2. For an **empty** deployment, run one gateway once with `CATALOG_INITIALIZE=true` and `CATALOG_REDIS_URL` set. This creates an empty catalog only if absent.
3. Remove `CATALOG_INITIALIZE` before normal operation. Leaving it enabled would permit accidental reinitialization after data loss.
4. Start replicas with the same catalog URL/key and Qdrant configuration. Readiness checks now require an accessible, unlocked catalog; liveness remains independent.

Existing SQLite catalogs are **not automatically migrated**. Do not switch an existing deployment to an empty shared catalog: stop writes and export/validate the existing mappings, vector lists and aliases first. The versioned JSON format is `{ "indices": [["name", "mapping JSON", "vector-list JSON"]], "aliases": [["alias", "index"]] }`. Back up both stores, validate in staging, and only then switch all replicas together. Do not mix SQLite and shared-catalog replicas against the same collections.

For Helm, create a Secret containing the URL and set:

```yaml
replicaCount: 2
catalog:
  existingSecret: gateway-catalog
  existingSecretKey: redis-url
  key: 'qeg:{catalog}:v1'
persistence:
  enabled: false
```

Initialize the catalog separately before deploying these values. The chart deliberately never enables automatic initialization. It does not provision Redis/Valkey.

## Administration and recovery

Creating/deleting an index, changing mappings, or changing aliases acquires one non-expiring administrative claim. Another replica cannot mutate metadata concurrently; new requests fail closed while the claim exists. Requests already in flight may finish using their previously acquired mapping. A successful operation publishes the entire updated catalog and releases its claim in one Redis/Valkey script.

The claim deliberately has **no TTL**: expiring a lock while a slow or disconnected writer still changes Qdrant permits two administrators to act at once. An upstream error after a mutation was attempted, cancelled request, crash or ambiguous timeout therefore leaves the claim in place. Validation errors before an upstream mutation release the claim safely. The gateway returns the original error and logs that recovery is required. This prioritizes safe ownership over automatic availability.

Recovery requires an operator:

1. Stop all gateway replicas and ensure their outstanding Qdrant operations have completed.
2. Back up and inspect the catalog key and its `<catalog-key>:admin` claim. Compare the affected mappings/collections/aliases with Qdrant; resolve any partial creation/deletion or payload-index changes. A successful-but-unacknowledged commit may already have removed the claim.
3. Restore or repair the catalog to match the intended Qdrant state. Only after reconciliation, delete the administrative claim with Redis/Valkey's `DEL` command.
4. Restart the gateways and verify readiness and the affected operation.

Do not delete a claim while a writer may still be running. A Redis/Valkey transaction cannot atomically include Qdrant writes. This backend does not supply document `_create` or update compare-and-set across replicas, point-in-time search, exactly-once projections, multi-index aliases, or Lucene analyzer equivalence.

## Verification

Unit tests cover snapshot round-tripping, malformed metadata and administrative route classification. Run the real-server coordination test against a disposable Redis/Valkey instance:

```sh
CATALOG_TEST_REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:16379 cargo test shared_catalog -- --include-ignored
```

The tests check fresh cross-client reads, successful create/mapping/alias dispatch across independent replicas, concurrent administration exclusion, absence of lock expiry, wrong-owner rejection, safe validation-error release, capacity rejection before upstream writes and retention of a claim after its owner disappears. It creates unique temporary keys and deletes them on success.


Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/storage-findings.md

# storage-findings

# Storage findings

The storage comparison must include all durable data required by each architecture. For the gateway projection profile that means both Qdrant collections: the searchable collection and the low-overhead source collection. Gateway SQLite metadata is reported separately. Docker image layers and unused volume capacity are excluded.

## Fresh 500,000-document run

The containerized benchmark used the repository's standard profile, 500,000 generated products, 5,000-document bulk batches, 5,000 updates, and the two-collection gateway projection. The final mounted-directory measurements were:

| System | Storage | Size |
|---|---|---:|
| Native Elasticsearch | data directory | 16,500 KiB / 16.1 MiB |
| Gateway | Qdrant searchable collection | 502,064 KiB / 490.3 MiB |
| Gateway | Qdrant durable source collection | 209,088 KiB / 204.2 MiB |
| Gateway | gateway metadata | 24 KiB |
| Gateway total | searchable + source + metadata | 711,176 KiB / 694.5 MiB |

The complete gateway footprint was therefore approximately 43.1× the native Elasticsearch data directory in this run. This is not a defect to hide: Qdrant's segment and sparse-vector representation has a much larger fixed and per-document footprint for this small product schema, while Elasticsearch's on-disk representation is highly compact. The gateway's source projection is still useful for write-path isolation and stateless reads, but it is not currently a disk-saving strategy.

The same run measured 46.689 seconds versus 105.141 seconds for bulk setup, 191.52 ms versus 986.63 ms search P95 at 50 clients, and 522.68 versus 95.60 requests/second for the mixed workload. Single-document updates remained slower on the gateway. Both paths returned full source responses, but the top-ranked IDs were not identical.

## Payload minimization iteration

The projection layout was tightened after inspecting the payloads. The searchable collection no longer stores the full top-level source: it stores only the ID, index name, and mapped non-text fields needed by filters, sorts, and aggregations. The durable source collection stores only the ID, index name, and `_source`. Text remains in the sparse representation, and response hydration is unchanged.

A fresh 10,000-document run with the same benchmark client measured:

| Gateway layout | Qdrant data | Bulk setup | Single updates |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Two collections, minimized payloads | 15.9 MiB | 1.083 s | 1.210 s |
| One collection, source payload plus mapped filters | 13.6 MiB | 0.842 s | 0.814 s |

The one-collection profile is smaller for this tiny schema because it avoids the second collection's fixed segment overhead, but it gives up the source/search write separation. The minimized two-collection profile passed the same filter, GET, update, delete, source-response, and mixed-workload checks. The gateway now applies the same payload de-duplication principle to one-collection mode as well: only mapped non-text fields are mirrored beside `_source`. It is the better default when the goal is high read/mixed throughput and asynchronous projection updates; one collection remains a sensible option when disk footprint and update simplicity dominate.

The final 50,000-document scale check used the same client, 1,000 updates, 500 mixed requests, and 20 concurrent search clients:

| Profile | Qdrant data | Bulk setup | Updates | Search P95 | Mixed throughput |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| One collection | 60.6 MiB | 4.56 s | 1.88 s | 102.5 ms | 302 req/s |
| Two collections, minimized payloads | 73.8 MiB | 6.72 s | 2.81 s | 68.0 ms | 353 req/s |

This confirms the expected trade-off at a larger corpus: one collection saves about 18% of Qdrant storage and has a cheaper write path, while two collections deliver about 34% lower search P95 and 17% higher mixed throughput in this run.

This result also clarifies the tuning boundary: `on_disk` vectors and `m=0` are useful for keeping the source projection lightweight in memory, but they do not make Qdrant's segment representation smaller than Elasticsearch for this corpus. `on_disk_payload` can reduce resident memory pressure, but it is not expected to reduce durable bytes and may increase read latency. Payload indexes should therefore be created only for fields the application actually filters, sorts, or aggregates on.

## Design implication

The current recommendation is workload-dependent:

- Choose the gateway projection when search latency, mixed read throughput, memory headroom, and stateless horizontal scaling matter more than raw disk footprint.
- Keep native Elasticsearch as the stronger baseline when storage cost is dominant or ranked-result equivalence is a hard requirement.
- Do not enable a durable source projection merely to reduce storage. Enable it to isolate sparse-index work from source reads and to support asynchronous/eventual update strategies.
- For production sizing, repeat after Qdrant compaction and with the actual schema, payload indexes, replication factor, and retention policy. Update-heavy workloads must include post-compaction measurements because segment churn can temporarily inflate the footprint.

The reproducible collector is [benchmark/disk_usage.sh](https://dstockton.github.io/benchmark/disk_usage.sh). It measures mounted directories while the stack is running, so the result is tied to the actual persisted corpus rather than container limits or image size.

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-sorted-pages-look-past-first-candidates.md

# Find the next page across the whole catalogue

Sorting the first few candidates is not the same as finding the first few sorted
results. Likewise, asking for a page after price 20 cannot work reliably if the
gateway only fetched records priced below 20.

Filter-only searches with explicit field sorting now inspect every matching
Qdrant scroll page. The gateway keeps the best `from + size` candidates, drops
records before `search_after`, and continues until the scroll ends. Without
collapse, retained hit candidates are bounded by the requested window plus the
current upstream page.

```json
{"size":2,"sort":[{"rank":"asc"}],"search_after":[2]}
```

The six-document [comparison fixture](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/validation/aggregations)
expects records 3 and 4 from that request. It sends the same request to
Elasticsearch and to the gateway. A deterministic regression also puts the
cheapest record on a later page and verifies that it wins the first sorted page.

`post_filter` now scans beyond the initial candidate window too. Matching records
on later pages can fill the requested page, and the hit count covers the complete
post-filtered set. Aggregations continue to see the query before `post_filter`.

Run `cargo test aggregation_scroll_visits_every_page_and_uses_search_projection_values`
to exercise those cases without a running database.

This preserves stateless request handling: no server-side cursor session or Redis
entry is required. The trade-off is scanning matching records for each request.
Use a unique final sort field for predictable cursor boundaries. These changes
apply to filter-only searches; ranked text pagination retains its documented
candidate limits. Collapse still needs retained group members, so its memory cost
is different. Concurrent writes can move records between pages because this is
not a point in time snapshot.

The container replay against Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and Qdrant 1.19.2 passed all four cases: complete aggregations, post-filtered hits, the first sorted page, and its cursor continuation. The [captured results](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/aggregations/results.json) include actual request timings. They establish correctness for this fixture, not a speed advantage.

A later [three-engine benchmark](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-indexed-query-performance.md)
adds guarded indexed paths for compatible numeric sorting, keyword facets and
simple filter counts. The complete scan described here remains the fallback
when the gateway cannot prove those operations preserve the result.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-sharing-mappings-between-gateway-replicas.md

# Two gateways need one view of their mappings

Adding a second gateway sounds straightforward: start another process and send it traffic. But if each process has its own SQLite file, an alias created through one process is invisible to the other. A restart-safe local database does not automatically become shared metadata.

Qdrant ES Gateway now has an optional Redis/Valkey catalog for that deployment. Mappings, vector names and aliases live in one authoritative store. Each request reads its current committed catalog, so the next request can land on either replica without relying on a local metadata cache. Qdrant continues to store the documents and perform searches.

SQLite remains the default. We have not measured a SQLite bottleneck, and there is no reason to add another service to a single-gateway setup just to replace a small local catalog.

## What changes for an operator

For a new empty deployment, configure `CATALOG_REDIS_URL`, initialize the catalog once with `CATALOG_INITIALIZE=true`, then remove that initialization flag and start the other replicas. Use a persistent, non-evicting Redis/Valkey deployment. Existing SQLite installations need a deliberate migration; simply pointing them at an empty catalog will not discover their mappings.

Administrative changes have one owner at a time. After a successful change, the gateway publishes the metadata and releases ownership atomically within Redis/Valkey. If a gateway crashes while changing a Qdrant collection, it leaves its administrative claim in place. New requests fail closed until an operator reconciles the two stores.

That recovery step is intentional. A lock that expires after thirty seconds does not prove a slow Qdrant request stopped executing. Letting another gateway take over at that point could make the catalog less trustworthy.

## What this does—and what it costs

The shared catalog solves visibility and administrative ownership. It does not turn Qdrant and Redis/Valkey into one transaction, or make concurrent document updates atomic. Nor is this a performance claim: every request fetches a bounded metadata snapshot and builds an ephemeral SQLite view. Large catalogs and high request rates need measurement before adopting this approach.

The real-server test uses two independent clients to verify that metadata becomes visible after commit, concurrent administrators are refused, and a vanished owner does not silently lose its claim. These are correctness checks, not benchmark results.

For configuration, the test command, durability requirements and the recovery procedure, see [the shared catalog guide](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/shared-catalog/). Start with SQLite for one gateway; choose shared metadata when adding replicas creates a real ownership problem.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-reading-reddit-with-an-honest-coverage-report.md

# Reading Reddit with an honest coverage report

A daily search investigation is only useful if we know what it actually read. Anonymous Reddit feeds returned HTTP 403 during ours. Cached search snippets sometimes showed conflicting relative dates. Neither was enough to establish that a report had been published in the previous 24 hours.

The repository now includes a small, read-only OAuth collector. Once Reddit approves the use and an account supplies a token, it walks the new-submission listings for Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, follows pagination, and selects reports using their exact UTC creation timestamps. Duplicate IDs, removed posts, and old pinned entries do not become fresh reports.

Run `python3 scripts/reddit_reports.py --metadata-only` to get a coverage manifest for the preceding 24 hours. Each subreddit records how many pages were read and why reading stopped. A page cap, repeated cursor, or access error produces an incomplete status and a failing exit code. An exhausted listing means that accessible listing ended; it does not mean every Reddit conversation was reviewed.

The offline tests exercise pagination, time boundaries, duplicate reports, deleted bodies, and partial listings. Live OAuth collector access has not been verified. Reddit says, [“Clients must authenticate with a registered OAuth token.”](https://support.reddithelp.com/hc/en-us/articles/16160319875092-Reddit-Data-API-Wiki) Its [Responsible Builder Policy](https://support.reddithelp.com/hc/en-us/articles/42728983564564-Responsible-Builder-Policy) also requires approval for the use case. The collector cannot grant that approval.

There is no persistent content cache. Titles and bodies are available for immediate review, while metadata-only output omits them. Anyone retaining output or publishing a quotation must handle deletion and the applicable retention terms. The [setup guide](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/research/README.md) includes a transparent access-request description covering automated technical assessment and possible articles.

This improves the evidence trail, not the gateway's query speed. When a source remains inaccessible, the investigation will say so instead of treating an empty search result as proof that nobody had a problem.

A follow-up browser check reached the Elasticsearch listing using the account owner's existing Chrome profile. This gives the investigation another way to read public threads when anonymous requests fail. It also exposed a different limit: the OpenSearch subreddit displayed a banned-community notice. Browser access and approved API access are separate paths, and neither makes a banned community available. We record which path supplied each source and never extract browser session credentials.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-measuring-small-read-path-changes.md

# Fewer requests did not make this query faster

We tried to speed up gateway aggregations by combining their safety checks.
Two filter counts would need four Qdrant calls instead of five, including the
exact total. That sounded promising. After measuring the final implementation,
we removed it: fewer calls did not produce a reliable latency improvement, and
filter counts were slightly slower.

This followed our [indexed-query optimization](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-indexed-query-performance.md).
The large win there came from avoiding a complete document scan. The next round
was about much smaller costs: database query preparation, duplicated payloads,
and coordination between independent reads.

### Compare the code, not the warmup

Fresh runs changed the ranking even when the gateway binary stayed identical.
We therefore kept the same 10,000 documents and alternated the old and new
images in **old, new, new, old** order. Each round shuffled Elasticsearch,
OpenSearch and gateway + Qdrant trials, used persistent connections, and warmed
each workload before measuring it. No image builds ran during these trials.

The retained read-path change passed **72,000 measured response checks** across
four rounds. That includes full sources, IDs, ordering, exact totals and buckets.
Each variant contributes six trial medians to each table cell; values are
**one client / eight clients**, in milliseconds.

| Gateway operation | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.380 / 0.781 | 0.370 / 0.783 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 0.702 / 2.055 | 0.688 / 2.037 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 1.022 / 2.613 | 1.009 / 2.521 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.892 / 3.382 | 0.896 / 3.159 |
| Two filter counts | 1.109 / 3.332 | 1.129 / 3.283 |

These small, mixed differences do not establish a broad speedup. Native engines
remained faster in all ten workload/concurrency combinations in this warmed
comparison. The [complete summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-read-path/summary.json)
includes their results, p95 latency, throughput and trial ranges.

### What we kept

Document reads now ask Qdrant only for the payload fields they consume. For one
representative benchmark document, the internal payload shrank from **684 to
274 bytes**, while the returned source stayed identical. Bulk existence checks
request only document IDs. GET and HEAD no longer parse unused mapping metadata;
SQLite reuses prepared statements, and parsing happens outside the catalog lock.
The final search page also takes ownership of its hits instead of copying them.

These remove specific work without a result cache or another service. Alias
changes still take effect immediately: prepared statements cache query plans,
not catalog answers. The evidence supports reduced data movement; it does not
support a promised percentage improvement in application latency.

### What we rejected

The combined aggregation check required a more complicated backend predicate.
Review also caught an intermediate-memory problem with launching every facet at
once. We bounded concurrency and reduced responses immediately, then reran the
comparison. The final result still did not justify the extra complexity, so the
original aggregation path remains. CPU redistribution, one runtime worker and
an exploratory in-memory payload configuration also failed to establish a
consistent benefit; their defaults remain unchanged.

Native caching matters, but it is not the whole explanation. Both native engines
recorded roughly 18,000 request-cache hits and three misses. [Elasticsearch](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/shard-request-cache.html)
and [OpenSearch](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/search-plugins/caching/request-cache/)
cache eligible aggregation requests by default.
A separate `request_cache=false` diagnostic left those counters unchanged, yet
native engines remained faster. Adding Redis without locating the remaining
cost would not by itself solve that difference.

### Reproduce the read comparison

Build both gateway revisions before timing, load the shared corpus using the
[three-engine runner](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/benchmark/three-engine),
and replace only the gateway image between rounds. Retain the data volumes and
wait for readiness after each replacement.

```sh
ROUND=baseline-a REQUESTS=200 TRIALS=3 WARMUP=40 \
  OUTPUT=results/baseline-a.json python3 compare_reads.py
# Repeat with candidate-b, candidate-c and baseline-d.
python3 summarize_reads.py results/baseline-a.json results/baseline-d.json
python3 summarize_reads.py results/candidate-b.json results/candidate-c.json
```

Every engine receives the same requests; the original aggregate two-CPU, 4-GiB
limits remain. The [evidence manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-read-path/manifest.json)
identifies revisions, raw round files, image IDs and the rejected experiment.
This remains an investigation, not a claim that the gateway has overtaken the
native engines.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-indexed-query-performance.md

# Sorting twenty records should not fetch ten thousand

Our first three-engine benchmark exposed a straightforward problem. To return
20 sorted products, the gateway fetched all 10,000 matching documents from
Qdrant. It also fetched those documents to count a handful of categories.
The answers were correct, but moving and reducing all that data was expensive:
median sorted-page latency was 55.6 ms, and terms aggregation took 39.1 ms.
Elasticsearch and OpenSearch completed those operations in roughly 1–2 ms.

We changed where the work happens. For compatible numeric fields, Qdrant now
orders the records and returns the requested page. Keyword buckets use exact
Qdrant facets; simple filter counts use its count API. Independent reads run
concurrently, and a count-only request does not fetch an unused document.
No client request changes, result cache, or Redis/Valkey service were needed.

Each cell shows **one client / eight clients**, in milliseconds.

| Operation | Elasticsearch | OpenSearch | Gateway + Qdrant |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.466 / 1.194 | 0.428 / 1.047 | 0.502 / 1.298 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 1.023 / 2.960 | 0.939 / 3.251 | 0.917 / 3.190 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 0.948 / 2.263 | 0.733 / 2.602 | 1.228 / 3.565 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.586 / 1.996 | 0.605 / 1.791 | 1.068 / 4.302 |
| Two filter counts | 0.714 / 2.928 | 0.718 / 2.854 | 1.135 / 4.167 |

These are median trial p50 latencies in milliseconds, measured with one and
eight concurrent clients. Every measured response passed correctness checks:
IDs, full sources, sort values, exact totals, bucket order and counts. We kept
all trials, including slower ones. The [full summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15/summary.json)
contains p95 latency, throughput and the range of trial medians.

The optimized gateway reduced observed sorted-page latency to 1.228 ms,
about 45 times lower than the first run. Native engines also became faster
across runs, so that ratio is an observed before/after result, not an isolated
production speedup guarantee. The gateway narrowly led filtered search at one
client; that small margin is not a broad performance win. In this measured run, native engines had lower median latency in nine of the ten
workload/concurrency combinations. They also led searchable ingest throughput: roughly
31,900 documents/s for Elasticsearch, 41,600 for OpenSearch and 22,600 for the
gateway.

The clearer advantage was the observed memory footprint. During separate
five-second, eight-client filter-count probes, gateway + Qdrant used about
327 MiB, versus 973 MiB for Elasticsearch and 912 MiB for OpenSearch. Those are
single Docker memory observations, not peaks or production sizing estimates.
For a compact catalogue service already using Qdrant, this is a useful trade:
near-millisecond scalar queries with a smaller observed footprint. For the
lowest latency or fastest ingest in this profile, the native engines remain
stronger choices.

There is a correctness condition behind the speedup. New writes record which
fields have values the indexed operation can handle exactly. Queries check that
coverage before using the fast result. Old documents, mixed types, missing
numeric values, multiple sort fields and page-boundary ties use the complete
scan. Existing documents gain eligibility when rewritten; deploying the new
binary alone does not accelerate every old index. Existing indexes that already
own the new internal field retain their
original data and behavior. This remains stateless request processing; it does
not turn pagination into a snapshot during concurrent writes.

### Reproduce the comparison

The [container profile and runner](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/benchmark/three-engine)
use Elasticsearch 8.15.0, OpenSearch 3.9.0 and Qdrant 1.19.2. Each native engine
