has a two-CPU, 4-GiB cap; Qdrant and the gateway share the same total cap. Both
JVM heaps are 512 MiB. The dataset has 10,000 deterministic documents with
integer rank/price fields, 20 keyword categories and a description. All engines
receive the same mapping, documents and requests; only the endpoint changes.
This tests scalar catalogue operations, not text relevance or vector search.

```sh
cd benchmark/three-engine
docker compose -p qeg-balanced -f compose.yml up -d --build
# Once all three endpoints respond:
DOCS=10000 TRIALS=3 REQUESTS=40 CONCURRENCY=1,8 python3 run.py
python3 summarize.py results/three-engine.json
```

The runner uses persistent HTTP connections, warms each workload, shuffles engine
order with a fixed seed, and measures three trials of 40 requests. Bulk timings
include waiting until all documents are searchable. It deletes only its named
benchmark index, so use the disposable containers. All services share one Docker
VM; this is a small reproducible lab profile, not a production capacity estimate.

Download the [baseline trials](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15/baseline.json),
[optimized trials](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15/optimized.json) and
[build/resource provenance](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15/provenance.json).
The practical improvement is that compatible catalogue queries move a page or
counts across the network instead of the entire matching catalogue. SQLite was
not the measured bottleneck, so replacing its small metadata catalog would not
have addressed the expensive work this benchmark revealed.

A [later paired comparison](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-measuring-small-read-path-changes.md)
examines warmup, native caches and smaller read-path changes.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-explicit-sparse-vectors-without-token-folding.md

# Keep your sparse token IDs intact

A sparse embedding is a small dictionary: token IDs paired with weights. If the
same token changes identity between indexing and searching, a successful HTTP
response can hide the wrong answer.

An [OpenSearch report](https://github.com/opensearch-project/neural-search/issues/2048)
describes exactly that problem in the SEISMIC approximate path of OpenSearch
3.9.0: “the query token is folded, the document tokens are not.” The report also
says the Lucene exact path returns the correct results.

The gateway now accepts explicit sparse embeddings and passes their numeric IDs
to Qdrant unchanged. IDs such as `32768`, `65535` and `65536` stay distinct.
Documents and queries share the same validation: canonical decimal IDs in the
unsigned 32-bit range and positive, finite float32 weights. Invalid vectors fail
before document writes. You supply embeddings; the gateway does not run a model.

Create a field with the common OpenSearch mapping shape:

```json
{"settings":{"index.sparse":true},"mappings":{"properties":{"v":{"type":"sparse_vector","method":{"name":"seismic","engine":"lucene"}}}}}
```

Index a document containing `{"v":{"65536":1.0}}`, then search:

```json
{"size":10,"query":{"neural_sparse":{"v":{"query_tokens":{"65536":1.0}}}}}
```

Qdrant executes an exact sparse dot product. The method labels in the mapping
are accepted compatibility syntax, not a request to run Lucene inside Qdrant.
Engine-specific tuning and model inference are rejected with a 400 response.

We checked the common request shape against real OpenSearch 3.9.0 and Qdrant
1.19.2. Eight documents used tokens `0`, `1`, `32767`, `32768`, `40342`, `65535`,
`65536` and `105878`. Every query returned exactly its own document on both
endpoints. This is a correctness check, **not a reproduction of the reported
approximate-path bug** or a speed comparison.

To repeat it from the repository checkout:

```sh
docker compose -f examples/explicit-sparse/compose.yml up -d --build
# Wait for both endpoints to answer GET /.
python3 examples/explicit-sparse/compare.py
docker compose -f examples/explicit-sparse/compose.yml down -v
```

The [demo and captured results](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/examples/explicit-sparse)
include the complete fixture and individual timings. The script sends identical
requests to both endpoints, changing only the endpoint address. It replaces its
own demo index, so run it against disposable instances.

For an application already using Qdrant, this adds an OpenSearch-shaped way to
search precomputed embeddings without another inference service or gateway
session store. It does not establish that migrating from OpenSearch is better:
the tested native exact path is correct too. Sparse queries currently support a
single top-level field and bounded `from`/`size`; total hits are a lower bound.
They reject aggregations, sorting, collapse, post-filtering, `min_score` and
`search_after`. Scalar filters on the sparse field also fail explicitly.
Use a new index when adding sparse fields to an existing mapping.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-documentation-you-can-read-as-text.md

# Documentation you can read as text

The blog works well in a browser. A coding assistant reviewing a migration needs something simpler: the compatibility boundary, the deployment instructions, and article text without navigation markup.

Every article now has a downloadable Markdown copy. The [llms.txt index](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/llms.txt) starts with the compatibility and production guides, then links to all articles. [llms-full.txt](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/llms-full.txt) puts those guides and the articles into one text file, with source links separating them.

These files are generated from the same Markdown sources that build the site. There is no second set of articles to maintain. Run `python3 scripts/export_agent_docs.py` after editing the documentation; `--check` detects stale copies in CI. The exports remove Jekyll front matter and resolve site links so a reader can follow them outside the rendered page.

The format follows the [llms.txt proposal](https://llmstxt.org/). It gives tools a predictable entry point; it does not guarantee that any crawler or assistant will discover, index, or follow it. Search engines can still use the normal HTML pages and sitemap.

For a migration review, start with the compatibility guide before reading a successful example. A post proves a particular workload, not full Elasticsearch or OpenSearch equivalence. Keeping that boundary beside the examples makes the repository easier to use responsibly, for people and agents alike.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-disabling-totals-should-not-slow-sorting.md

# Asking for less should not make sorting slower

A client that only needs the next page can set `track_total_hits: false` and
avoid asking for the total number of matching documents. In the gateway, that
apparently cheaper request had an expensive surprise: it disabled indexed
sorting and fetched every matching document from Qdrant instead.

On our 10,000-product catalogue, a single-client sorted page took **45.340 ms**.
After separating the sorting decision from the total-count decision, the same
request took **0.689 ms**. Both requests return the same twenty products, source
fields and sort values, with no `hits.total` field.

### Keep the page, skip the count

The gateway now uses its guarded indexed sorting path whether or not totals are
requested. When totals are disabled, it skips the exact count. A zero-size
aggregation response also skips the otherwise unused hit lookup. These are
request-local changes: no result cache, new database or Redis service is needed.

The existing safety checks still apply. Eligible scalar numeric fields can use
Qdrant's indexed ordering; unsupported values, old documents without eligibility
metadata and ambiguous page-boundary ties keep the complete-scan fallback.
Disabling totals does not relax sorting correctness or provide snapshot isolation
while documents change.

We measured **old, new, new, old** images against the same retained corpus. Each
image contributes six trial medians per table cell. Values below are median
trial p50 milliseconds, shown as **one client / eight clients**.

| Gateway operation, totals disabled | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.384 / 0.842 | 0.374 / 0.769 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 2.888 / 10.093 | 0.691 / 1.797 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 45.340 / 305.877 | 0.689 / 1.833 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.870 / 2.470 | 0.675 / 1.970 |
| Two filter counts | 1.102 / 3.305 | 0.858 / 2.954 |

The point-read request is unaffected by the totals option; its smaller movement
helps show ordinary measurement variation. The large sorting improvement removes
an identified full scan. It does **not** establish that the gateway is faster
than the native engines.

### Native engines still lead

All three engines received identical requests within this disabled-total profile;
only the endpoint changed. Here are the final candidate-round results, including
every workload rather than selecting the gateway's strongest result.

| Operation | Elasticsearch | OpenSearch | Gateway + Qdrant |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.307 / 0.599 | 0.289 / 0.579 | 0.374 / 0.769 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 0.487 / 1.082 | 0.468 / 1.020 | 0.691 / 1.797 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 0.554 / 1.185 | 0.442 / 1.028 | 0.689 / 1.833 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.355 / 0.863 | 0.354 / 0.856 | 0.675 / 1.970 |
| Two filter counts | 0.446 / 2.745 | 0.494 / 2.745 | 0.858 / 2.954 |

Both native engines remain faster in all ten workload/concurrency combinations.
For applications already using Qdrant, this fix makes requesting only a page
substantially more practical. It is not a reason to promise lower latency than
Elasticsearch or OpenSearch.

We separately repeated the four-round comparison with exact totals enabled.
That profile passed another 72,000 response checks, with no material measured
regression: single-client filtered search changed from 0.699 to 0.701 ms and
sorted pagination from 1.010 to 1.011 ms. Exact totals and disabled totals are
separate profiles; we did not give the gateway a cheaper request than its peers.
Across both profiles, **144,000 measured responses passed** checks for IDs, full
sources, ordering, bucket counts, and either exact totals or their absence.

### Reproduce it

Use the [three-engine harness](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/benchmark/three-engine)
with Elasticsearch 8.15.0, OpenSearch 3.9.0 and Qdrant 1.19.2. Build both gateway
images before timing and populate the disposable 10,000-document corpus once.
Each native engine has a two-CPU, 4-GiB cap; Qdrant and the gateway share the same
total cap. Native cache settings remain at their defaults.

```sh
# From benchmark/three-engine, after loading data and waiting for readiness:
TRACK_TOTAL_HITS=false ROUND=old-1 REQUESTS=200 TRIALS=3 WARMUP=40 \
  OUTPUT=results/old-1.json python3 compare_reads.py
# Replace only the gateway image, preserving volumes, and wait for readiness.
# Repeat as new-1, new-2, then old-2.
python3 summarize_reads.py results/old-1.json results/old-2.json
python3 summarize_reads.py results/new-1.json results/new-2.json
# Repeat all four rounds with TRACK_TOTAL_HITS=true into separate output files.
```

Each round interleaves all engines, uses persistent connections and warms every
trial. No builds or ingestion run during timing. The shared Docker host and small
scalar catalogue limit what these measurements establish; this is not a text,
vector, durability or production-capacity benchmark.

The [evidence manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-disabled-totals/manifest.json)
links all eight raw rounds, revisions and image provenance. Separate summaries
retain [disabled-total results](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-disabled-totals/disabled-summary.json)
and [exact-total results](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-disabled-totals/exact-summary.json),
including p95 latency, throughput and trial ranges. The improvement is concrete:
a client asking for less work no longer accidentally triggers a full scan.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-calendar-days-follow-local-time.md

# A reporting day is not always 24 hours

A sales report grouped by London day should move its boundaries when the clocks
change. Adding 86,400 seconds to yesterday's boundary gets that wrong twice a year.

The gateway now supports a small, explicit `date_histogram` subset: calendar days,
Monday-starting weeks, months, and years in an IANA time zone. It converts each
timestamp into local calendar time and converts that calendar boundary back to UTC.

```json
{"size":0,"aggs":{"sales_days":{"date_histogram":{"field":"date","calendar_interval":"day","time_zone":"Europe/London","min_doc_count":1}}}}
```

The deterministic test measures 23 hours between the March 29 and March 30, 2026
London boundaries and 25 hours between October 25 and October 26. Documents with
multiple timestamps count once per bucket. Run:

```sh
cargo test calendar_days_follow_dst_and_weeks_start_monday
```

The [comparison fixture](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/validation/aggregations)
contains dates on both sides of those transitions and sends identical requests to
Elasticsearch and the gateway. This is compatibility work for teams already using
Qdrant; there is no claimed speed advantage over a native calendar histogram.

Only nonempty buckets are supported, so `min_doc_count:1` is required. Custom
formats, fixed intervals, offsets, bounds, subaggregations, and nonexistent local
midnight boundaries fail explicitly. Input dates accept epoch milliseconds,
RFC3339 timestamps, and `YYYY-MM-DD` dates. Date-only input denotes midnight UTC.

Time-zone rules come from the compiled `chrono-tz` dependency. Keeping that data
current still matters: implementing a calendar reducer does not repair stale rules.
This does **not** claim to resolve the
[Graylog OpenSearch tzdata report](https://github.com/Graylog2/graylog2-server/issues/27755),
which describes "events near midnight land on the wrong day" under outdated rules.
That reported deployment needs separate reproduction with its exact engine and
updated zone data. The London checks exercise established DST rules, not those
reported Canadian and Moroccan rule changes.

The container replay against Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and Qdrant 1.19.2 passed all four cases: complete aggregations, post-filtered hits, the first sorted page, and its cursor continuation. The [captured results](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/aggregations/results.json) include actual request timings. They establish correctness for this fixture, not a speed advantage.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-aggregations-beyond-the-first-page.md

# The cheapest item may be on the next page

A price filter should describe the matching catalogue, even when the shopper only
asks for one product. The gateway previously calculated `min`, `max`, and filter
counts from the hit candidates it had fetched. A small `size` could therefore
produce a plausible but incomplete answer.

The fix separates those two jobs. Qdrant scrolls through every matching page;
the gateway retains the current extrema and bucket counters, then discards each
page. The hit limit no longer sets the scope of an aggregation. `post_filter`,
collapse, and `search_after` still affect hits, not aggregation membership.

For example:

```json
{"size":0,"aggs":{"lowest_price":{"min":{"field":"price"}},"brands":{"terms":{"field":"brand","size":2}}}}
```

Our regression puts prices 50 and 2 on separate pages. The result is 2, including
when the search returns no hits. Terms now count the complete matching set too,
deduplicate repeated values within one document, and report the actual count
outside the returned top buckets.

Run `cargo test aggregation_scroll_visits_every_page_and_uses_search_projection_values`
for the deterministic two-page check. The repository's
[`validation/aggregations` comparison](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/validation/aggregations)
also sends the same six-document fixture and requests to Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and
the gateway with Qdrant. It prints the observed results and individual timings.

This improves correctness within the gateway's supported subset; it is not a
claim that scanning is faster than Elasticsearch's native aggregations. A full
scan costs work proportional to the matching data. Metrics use constant state;
buckets have an explicit 10,000-distinct-value limit per aggregation and fail
rather than return truncated totals. There are at most 100 aggregations per request.

Ranked text and pattern queries are rejected when combined with aggregations,
because their candidate membership cannot currently be reduced exactly this way.
Concurrent writes can change a scroll while it runs. With document projection,
reductions use mapped non-text values in the search projection, keeping membership
and values together instead of fetching a newer source document.

The container replay against Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and Qdrant 1.19.2 passed all four cases: complete aggregations, post-filtered hits, the first sorted page, and its cursor continuation. The [captured results](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/aggregations/results.json) include actual request timings. They establish correctness for this fixture, not a speed advantage.

A later [three-engine benchmark](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-indexed-query-performance.md)
adds guarded indexed paths for compatible numeric sorting, keyword facets and
simple filter counts. The complete scan described here remains the fallback
when the gateway cannot prove those operations preserve the result.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-a-shared-catalog-is-not-a-snapshot.md

# A shared catalog is not a snapshot

Moving metadata out of a gateway process makes replicas easier to run. It does not make every Elasticsearch consistency promise available.

A `search_after` cursor describes where the next page should start. If documents change between pages, the next request sees those changes. A point-in-time search needs a retained view of the data, or retained results with clearly defined creation semantics. Saving a cursor in Valkey does not create that view.

The same distinction matters for writes. An `if_seq_no` and `if_primary_term` pair asks the engine to reject a write if the document changed. Checking a value in Redis and then writing to Qdrant is two operations across two systems. A failure or competing writer between them can break the promise. A fast key-value store cannot make them one transaction.

The gateway now rejects point-in-time search bodies and consistency-sensitive URL parameters before executing a request. For example, `PUT /products/_doc/1?if_seq_no=0&if_primary_term=1` returns a structured `400` instead of silently performing an unconditional write. Explicit routing, external versions, scroll contexts, and conflict retries are also rejected when supplied as URL parameters. The focused tests check encoded parameter names as well as ordinary requests.

This keeps the boundary visible while shared metadata and stateless query translation improve. Atomic concurrent document updates still need an authoritative conditional-write mechanism and recovery design. Full Lucene phrase semantics need positional indexing. Neither is supplied by adding a metadata cache.

For applications that use only the supported subset, Qdrant can remain the document and retrieval engine while gateway replicas keep no durable local catalog. Applications requiring snapshot pagination or concurrent compare-and-set writes should retain their native engine for those operations until the gateway can demonstrate the same guarantee.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-14-index-names-are-a-client-contract.md

# Index names are a client contract

An invalid index name used to make it through the gateway's metadata catalogue and into a normalized Qdrant collection name. That was more than cosmetic. An application could successfully provision state that the same Elasticsearch or OpenSearch client would expect a native cluster to reject, and distinct punctuation could then collide in Qdrant's namespace.

Elasticsearch and OpenSearch implement their validators independently, so this change checked both rather than assuming the fork still behaved like its ancestor. [Elasticsearch 9.5.5's validator](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v9.5.5/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/cluster/metadata/MetadataCreateIndexService.java#L342-L365) and [OpenSearch 3.9's validator](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/blob/3.9/server/src/main/java/org/opensearch/cluster/metadata/MetadataCreateIndexService.java#L313-L342) agree on the static boundary:

- a name must be non-empty and lowercase;
- filesystem-reserved punctuation, `#`, and `:` are forbidden;
- `_`, `-`, and `+` cannot be the first character;
- the UTF-8 encoding cannot exceed 255 bytes; and
- `.` and `..` are invalid.

The byte boundary matters for non-ASCII names: 127 copies of `é` occupy 254 UTF-8 bytes and pass, while 128 copies occupy 256 bytes and fail. The source implementations permit `+` away from the first character, despite the current OpenSearch prose documentation listing `+` among generally forbidden characters. The gateway follows the versioned 3.9 implementation for that edge rather than broadening the rejection.

Invalid create requests now return HTTP 400 with the client-recognizable `invalid_index_name_exception`, root cause, index name, and `_na_` index UUID. Validation runs under the existing index-administration lock but before SQLite reads and Qdrant requests. Focused regressions cover the UTF-8 byte limit, punctuation, prefixes, lowercase requirement, response shape, and a zero-request mock upstream counter:

```console
cargo test index_name_validation_matches_shared_native_rules
cargo test invalid_index_creation_fails_before_qdrant_work
```

This run is source- and request-level validation, not a live-engine benchmark. The local Docker service did not answer its availability check, so no native containers were claimed. Dot-prefixed names other than the exact `.` and `..` remain accepted by both versioned static validators; their separate hidden/system-index checks and deprecation behavior are not emulated by the gateway.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-14-alias-options-must-not-disappear.md

# Alias options must not disappear

The gateway deliberately implements unfiltered, unrouted aliases with one concrete target. Its alias action parser previously read only `index` and `alias`, but silently ignored every other metadata field. A request for a tenant filter, custom routing, or a write index could therefore return `{"acknowledged":true}` while the stored alias exposed all documents and routed every operation normally. That is more dangerous than an unsupported-feature error because the response tells the caller that a data-access or write-routing boundary exists when it does not.

Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 expose the same relevant action fields, but they were checked independently. The versioned [Elasticsearch request parser](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v9.5.5/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/action/admin/indices/alias/IndicesAliasesRequest.java#L98-L108) accepts `filter`, `routing`, `index_routing`, `search_routing`, `is_write_index`, and `is_hidden` for add actions, plus `must_exist` for removals. The versioned [OpenSearch request parser](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/blob/3.9.0/server/src/main/java/org/opensearch/action/admin/indices/alias/IndicesAliasesRequest.java#L106-L116) declares the corresponding fields, and the separate [OpenSearch alias documentation](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/api-reference/alias/aliases-api/) describes their effects. This is source-level evidence for the two engines, not an assumption that verification against one applies to the other.

The gateway now rejects every action metadata field outside its supported `index` and `alias` subset. Known native options and unknown fields receive a structured HTTP 400 naming the exact path, such as `_aliases.add.filter` or `_aliases.remove.must_exist`. Validation happens before index lookup and before the SQLite transaction, so a rejected request cannot create, remove, or modify an alias and never contacts Qdrant.

```console
cargo test alias_actions_reject_options_the_gateway_cannot_apply
```

The regression covers filters, all three routing forms, write-index and hidden flags, removal `must_exist`, and an unknown option. It also asserts that the catalogue still contains only its original alias after all failures. Docker was not responsive during this run, so no live Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or Qdrant endpoint result is claimed. This change does not add filtered, routed, hidden, or multi-index aliases; it makes the existing compatibility boundary honest and fail closed.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-13-creating-an-index-is-not-a-mapping-update.md

# Creating an index is not a mapping update

Provisioning code often treats “already exists” as a narrow, recoverable race. It can do that reliably only when the server identifies the condition correctly. The gateway already rejected a second `PUT /products` before contacting Qdrant, but it grouped the request with unsupported query features and returned `qdrant_gateway_unsupported_query`. That classification could make an Elasticsearch or OpenSearch client treat a normal create race as an incompatible request.

Elasticsearch and OpenSearch implement this case independently but agree on the exception class. [Elasticsearch 9.5.5's create-index service](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v9.5.5/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/cluster/metadata/MetadataCreateIndexService.java#L291-L295) throws `ResourceAlreadyExistsException` when either routing or index metadata already contains the name. [OpenSearch 3.9's corresponding service](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/blob/3.9/server/src/main/java/org/opensearch/cluster/metadata/MetadataCreateIndexService.java#L275-L279) performs the same two checks. OpenSearch also publishes the resulting REST example as HTTP 400 with `resource_already_exists_exception` in its [create/delete error-shape discussion](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/issues/14805).

The gateway now returns the shared client-visible shape, including a root cause, top-level exception, reason, index name, and status 400. The check runs under the existing index-administration lock and before any Qdrant request. A focused regression also proves that the original mapping remains unchanged:

```console
cargo test duplicate_index_creation_returns_native_conflict_without_qdrant_work
```

This is request-level validation with a mocked upstream request counter, not a live-engine benchmark. Cached Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 containers were available for a native probe, but the local Docker storage backend returned an input/output error before either container started. The version-specific source above is therefore the native evidence for this run. The gateway does not include a native index UUID because its metadata catalogue does not currently assign one. A different requested name that merely normalizes to an occupied Qdrant collection remains a gateway-specific `index.name` validation error rather than pretending that the Elasticsearch/OpenSearch index itself already exists.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-13-alias-add-is-not-a-retarget.md

# Alias add is not a retarget

The gateway stores one concrete index per alias. Its alias transaction used SQLite `INSERT OR REPLACE` for an `add` action, so adding an existing alias to a different index silently discarded the original target. That looked like a convenient retarget, but it changed the meaning of a standard Elasticsearch/OpenSearch request and could redirect application reads and writes without the caller expressing a swap.

A direct endpoint probe against Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 used the same five-request sequence: create `products-v1` and `products-v2`, add `current-products` to the first, add it to the second, then inspect the alias. Both native engines acknowledged both adds and returned both indices as targets. This agrees with the independent [Elasticsearch alias documentation](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/aliases.html) and [OpenSearch manage-aliases documentation](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/api-reference/alias/aliases-api/): aliases can cover multiple indices, and a move is expressed as remove plus add in one atomic request. The sanitized [probe evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/elasticsearch-9.5.5-opensearch-3.9-alias-add-2026-10-13.json) records the versions, requests, acknowledgements, and final targets.

The gateway still deliberately supports only single-target aliases. It now evaluates the final topology of the complete action batch before opening the write transaction. An add-only request that would require two targets receives a structured HTTP 400 compatibility error, and the existing target remains unchanged. A remove+add swap remains accepted in either action order because the final topology has one target and the SQLite transaction makes the change atomically visible.

```console
cargo test alias_add_does_not_silently_retarget_a_single_index_alias
```

This is a fail-closed compatibility improvement, not multi-index alias support. The gateway does not yet merge searches across indices, select a write index, apply alias filters, or reproduce native per-action partial-failure responses. The endpoint probe measures request semantics only; it makes no latency or resource-use claim.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-12-head-must-not-hide-storage-failures.md

# HEAD must not hide storage failures

Document-existence checks have a deliberately small contract. The [Elasticsearch 8 API reference](https://www.elastic.co/docs/api/doc/elasticsearch/v8/operation/operation-exists) and the [OpenSearch Get Document API reference](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/api-reference/document-apis/get-documents/#checking-document-existence) both describe `HEAD /<index>/_doc/<id>` as HTTP 200 when the document exists and HTTP 404 when it does not. A storage outage is neither result.

The gateway's HEAD path previously caught every Qdrant error and returned 404. A connection failure, missing collection, or Qdrant 5xx therefore looked like a trustworthy “document absent” answer. That can make health checks, conditional writes, and reconciliation jobs take destructive action on false information.

HEAD now uses the same narrow missing-point classification as GET without retrieving the document source. The known Qdrant missing-point response remains a 404, while transport failures and upstream errors return 502. All gateway HEAD routes also attach `X-Elastic-Product: Elasticsearch`, and the response body remains empty. The focused regression injects a Qdrant 503 and verifies an empty 502 response in both embedded-source and document-projection modes:

```console
cargo test head_document_does_not_hide_qdrant_failures_as_not_found
```

This validation is request-level and uses a mocked Qdrant response; it is not a live Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or Qdrant benchmark. The native status contract comes from the public engine documentation above. Query parameters such as `routing`, `refresh`, `realtime`, and explicit version checks remain outside the gateway's current HEAD compatibility surface.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-12-a-missing-point-is-not-a-failed-upstream.md

# A missing point is not a failed upstream

The Elasticsearch and OpenSearch index APIs are upserts, but their response describes which side of the operation happened. Live probes against Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 both returned HTTP 201 with `result: "created"` for the first `PUT /<index>/_doc/<id>`, then HTTP 200 with `result: "updated"` for the replacement.

The gateway already performed a point read before this write so it could make the same distinction. Against the repository's pinned Qdrant 1.15.5, however, a missing single point returns HTTP 404 with a structured “Point with id … does not exists” error. The generic Qdrant client treated every non-success response as an upstream failure, so the very first index request returned 502 and never reached the upsert.

Single-point reads now recognize that exact missing-point response as an absent document. The shared path fixes ordinary GETs and the preflight reads used by standalone index, create, update, and delete operations. The exception is deliberately narrow: a Qdrant 404 that says the collection is missing still becomes a gateway 502, preserving a visible signal for storage/catalogue drift instead of pretending the document is absent.

The sanitized [Elasticsearch 9.5.5, OpenSearch 3.9.0, and Qdrant 1.15.5 evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/elasticsearch-9.5.5-opensearch-3.9-qdrant-missing-point-2026-10-12.json) records the native contract, Qdrant response shape, and live changed-gateway results. The gateway returned 404 for a missing GET, 201/`created` for the first PUT, 200/`updated` for the second PUT, and the replacement source on the final GET. Focused regressions use the observed Qdrant error body in both source-storage modes and prove that missing collections remain upstream errors.

This is a single-document correctness check, not a concurrency or performance benchmark. The extra existence read was already part of the standalone index path, so the fix adds no request. That preflight still is not an atomic compare-and-write across gateway replicas, and the gateway's sequence-number, primary-term, and version fields remain approximate.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-11-source-filters-should-not-leak-siblings.md

# Source filters should not leak sibling fields

Elasticsearch clients often use `_source` filtering to keep response payloads small or avoid returning fields a particular view does not need. The gateway accepted array-shaped top-level filters, but a string such as `"profile.name"` silently returned the complete source. Nested paths were compared only with top-level keys, so even some accepted filters returned the wrong shape. A caller asking for a profile name could therefore receive sibling contact fields or unrelated metadata.

A live probe against native Elasticsearch 9.5.5 established four narrow response contracts. A single dotted field returned `{"profile":{"name":"Ada"}}`; `profile.contact.*` preserved the nested contact object; an include of `profile.*` plus an exclusion of `profile.contact.phone` retained the email but removed the phone; and a numeric `_source` value failed with HTTP 400. The changed gateway produced the same shapes against pinned Qdrant 1.15.5. The sanitized [endpoint evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/elasticsearch-9.5.5-source-filtering-2026-10-11.json) records the fixture, requests, statuses, and projected sources.

The gateway now parses source filters before index lookup or Qdrant access, supports string and string-array patterns plus the singular and plural include/exclude options, and reconstructs nested objects while applying `*` and `?` wildcards. Collapse inner hits use the same parser. Malformed or mixed-type filters fail rather than falling back to the full source.

This is response minimization, not field-level authorization. The gateway still hydrates the complete source before applying the filter, so source filtering does not reduce Qdrant read bandwidth or in-process memory use. The probe covers nested objects and common wildcard forms, not every Elasticsearch source-filtering edge case. OpenSearch was not run, so this result does not claim OpenSearch parity.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-11-integer-hit-totals-need-the-minus-one-sentinel.md

# Integer hit totals need the minus-one sentinel

OpenSearch retains a legacy response mode for clients that expect `hits.total` to be a number rather than the newer `{value, relation}` object. A live probe against OpenSearch 3.9.0 confirmed that `rest_total_hits_as_int=true` returns the exact integer for an ordinary search and the sentinel `-1` when the request also sets `track_total_hits: false`. The same query parameter applies to every item in `_msearch`. The gateway previously discarded the query string, so these requests silently received the wrong response shape.

The gateway now carries the parameter through both endpoints, returns integer totals and the native disabled sentinel, and preserves the existing object shape for `false` or an absent parameter. Parsing matches the observed OpenSearch boundary: lowercase `true` and `false` are accepted, an empty or valueless parameter enables the mode, duplicate parameters use the last value, and a numeric `track_total_hits` threshold combined with integer formatting fails before index lookup or Qdrant work because the requested format cannot represent an inexact threshold.

The sanitized [OpenSearch 3.9.0 evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/opensearch-3.9-rest-total-hits-as-int-2026-10-11.json) records six `_search` cases and the two `_msearch` totals over three documents. A live gateway backed by pinned Qdrant 1.15.5 matched those shapes; focused tests also cover strict parsing, duplicate parameters, fail-fast validation, and upstream request counts.

This is response-shape compatibility, not a performance benchmark. Integer totals have no place to carry the gateway's normal `eq` or `gte` relation, so callers using bounded text-search paths should prefer the object form when accuracy metadata matters. Elasticsearch was not run for this note, and no cross-engine parity claim is made.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-10-disabled-hit-totals-should-skip-the-count.md

# Disabled hit totals should skip the count

OpenSearch lets a search caller choose the cost and precision of `hits.total`. A live probe against OpenSearch 3.6.0 with 15 matching documents confirmed the three useful modes: the default returned `15/eq`, `track_total_hits: false` omitted `hits.total`, a threshold of 5 returned `5/gte`, and a threshold of 20 returned `15/eq`. The gateway previously ignored all four request shapes and always paid for its exact Qdrant count on eligible filter-only searches.

The gateway now accepts boolean and non-negative integer modes. Disabling totals omits the response field and, importantly, skips the exact-count request. A live gateway backed by the repository's pinned Qdrant 1.15.5 image matched all four OpenSearch response shapes after write visibility converged. A request-level regression with a mocked Qdrant endpoint records one upstream scroll request instead of the usual count plus scroll pair. Numeric thresholds cap exact or bounded totals and preserve an honest `eq` or `gte` relation.

The [saved native-engine evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/opensearch-3.6-track-total-hits-2026-10-10.json) contains the fixture and response values without endpoint or container identifiers. This is a request-count result, not a latency benchmark: the actual saving depends on collection size, filters, Qdrant load, and network placement.

There are two deliberate boundaries. A numeric threshold shapes the gateway response but does not terminate Qdrant's exact count early, so only `false` has a demonstrated upstream request saving. OpenSearch 3.6.0 also coerced some undocumented string, fractional, and negative values during the probe; the gateway accepts the documented boolean and non-negative integer forms and rejects other types before index lookup or Qdrant work. Elasticsearch was not run for this field note, so the native evidence here is OpenSearch-specific even though the supported request forms are shared by both APIs.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-09-search-after-needs-more-than-one-page.md

# Search-after needs more than one page

A deterministic catalogue replay against native Elasticsearch 9.5.5 exposed an empty second page from the gateway. Six products were sorted by ascending price, the first two sort values were returned as the cursor, and Elasticsearch returned the next two products. The gateway returned none.

The cursor comparison itself was correct. The gateway had asked Qdrant for only `size` candidates, sorted those candidates locally, and then tried to find a cursor from the previous request inside that new first-page-sized set. The same boundary could also make the first sorted page depend on Qdrant's unrelated point order.

Explicitly sorted searches now retrieve a candidate window of at least the configured `MAX_PAGE_SIZE` before ordering and applying `search_after`. A request-level regression uses a Qdrant mock that really truncates its response to the requested limit; with a three-candidate window, a two-hit first page and its cursor produce the remaining document. The live replay with the default 1,000-candidate window improved from 10/12 to 11/12 checks against Elasticsearch 9.5.5. The saved [endpoint evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/elasticsearch-9.5.5-2026-10-09.json) records the exact requests, endpoint identities, and one-second gateway convergence allowance.

This is bounded compatibility, not global Qdrant field ordering. A cursor cannot advance beyond the configured candidate window, changes to that window can invalidate a cursor, and each explicitly sorted request can now retrieve and hydrate up to `MAX_PAGE_SIZE` candidates even when the returned page is small. The remaining replay difference is the already documented analyzer boundary: Elasticsearch's lowercase prefix over a `text` field matches `Wireless`, while gateway-side stored-source matching remains case-sensitive. This run validated Elasticsearch 9.5.5; it did not treat the prior OpenSearch 3.6.0 replay as proof of identical server behavior.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-09-opensearch-wildcards-keep-the-leading-star.md

# OpenSearch wildcards keep the leading star

A catalogue replay against native OpenSearch 3.6.0 found a gateway-only empty result for `{"wildcard":{"title":"*keyboard*"}}`. The document was present and other filters worked. The defect was in the gateway's wildcard-to-regular-expression translation: a leading `*` disappeared, turning a contains query into a starts-with query.

The translator now handles the pattern one character at a time. `*` becomes any-length text, `?` becomes one character, and every other character is escaped as a literal. A focused regression covers leading, trailing, and consecutive stars, `?`, and regular-expression punctuation in source text.

The reproducible endpoint replay used native OpenSearch 3.6.0, Qdrant ES Gateway from this change, and the repository's pinned Qdrant 1.15.5 image. With a one-second post-ingest settle, 10 of 12 application checks passed after the fix. The remaining differences are explicit limitations: a lowercase prefix over an analyzed OpenSearch `text` field does not match the gateway's mixed-case stored source, and gateway-side `search_after` ordering operates over a bounded candidate window. The saved [request-level evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/opensearch-3.6-2026-10-09.json) records both endpoint identities, requests, responses, and the settle interval.

The settle is part of the result, not a hidden correction. OpenSearch honored `refresh=wait_for`; the gateway's sparse search projection still needs a convergence allowance. The replay now records that allowance and sends `refresh=wait_for` for the final delete on both endpoints, preventing unmatched refresh timing from masquerading as a count incompatibility.

The current official Python client was checked separately at the transport boundary: `opensearch-py` 3.2.0 completed info, index creation, bulk indexing, search, count, update, get, and delete against the gateway. That is client-shape evidence, not a claim that the gateway identifies itself as OpenSearch or implements the full OpenSearch API.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-08-invalid-pages-should-not-query-qdrant.md

# Invalid pages should not query Qdrant

Pagination inputs sit on a resource boundary. [Elasticsearch documents `from` as non-negative, `size` as non-negative, and `search_after` as an array of scalar sort values](https://www.elastic.co/docs/api/doc/elasticsearch/operation/operation-search). It also limits the ordinary `from` plus `size` result window to 10,000 by default and directs deeper pagination to `search_after`.

The gateway previously used defaults when `from` or `size` had the wrong JSON type, silently capped an oversized `size`, ignored a non-array `search_after`, and fetched candidates from Qdrant before discovering some cursor shape errors. Those responses could look valid while representing a different page from the one requested, and malformed requests still consumed upstream work.

Search pagination now passes through one fail-fast validator before index lookup or Qdrant access. `from` and `size` must be non-negative integers, `size` cannot exceed the configured `MAX_PAGE_SIZE`, and `from + size` cannot exceed 10,000. `search_after` requires one string, number, boolean, or null per explicit sort field and cannot be combined with a non-zero offset. A regression sends malformed and over-limit variants to a mock Qdrant server and verifies both the structured compatibility error and a zero upstream request count.

```bash
cargo test invalid_pagination_fails_before_qdrant_work
cargo test --all-targets --all-features
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
```

This is validation, not unbounded pagination. The gateway still sorts only the bounded candidate window it retrieves, its 10,000 result-window boundary is fixed rather than index-configurable, and its cursor is stable only while that ordered set is unchanged. `MAX_PAGE_SIZE` may be set below 10,000 as a stricter operator-controlled resource limit.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-08-inner-hits-need-the-requested-name.md

# Inner hits need the requested name

The AWS Retail Demo Store sends a normal Elasticsearch collapse request: collapse on `category.keyword`, name the inner result `category_hits`, request a bounded number of group members, and suppress `_source`. Its response code then reads `item["inner_hits"]["category_hits"]` to distribute products across categories. The request is visible in the project's [search service](https://github.com/aws-samples/retail-demo-store/blob/master/src/search/src/search-service/app.py#L130-L158), and the corresponding response access is a few lines below.

The gateway previously treated every property inside the `inner_hits` definition as if it were an inner-hit name. A request containing `name`, `size`, `fields`, and `_source` therefore returned groups with those literal keys instead of `category_hits`. It also left `_source` in nested hits even when the inner definition disabled it. The request returned HTTP 200, but the unchanged application could not consume the response.

Collapse parsing now happens before index lookup or Qdrant access. The gateway emits the requested inner-hit name, honors the inner size and source projection independently from the top-level projection, accepts the application's `_id` metadata-field request, and caps inner results with `MAX_PAGE_SIZE`. Unsupported options fail with a structured 400 rather than being silently ignored.

The regression uses the public application's exact collapse shape over three mocked products in two categories. It verifies two collapsed top-level hits, a two-document `category_hits` group, correct IDs, no leaked `_source`, and zero Qdrant requests for invalid or over-limit collapse options:

```sh
cargo test retail_collapse_inner_hits_use_the_requested_name_size_and_source_filter
cargo test invalid_collapse_fails_before_qdrant_work
```

This remains deliberately bounded compatibility. The gateway currently accepts one inner-hit definition, does not implement inner-hit sorting, and groups only the retrieved candidate window. Group totals are exact within that window, not across all matches in a large index. Those limits are now explicit instead of being hidden behind a response shape that the target application could not read.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-07-post-filters-must-fail-closed.md

# Unsupported post filters must fail closed

The gateway documents a deliberately small `post_filter` subset: term, terms, numeric range, exists, match-all, and bool combinations of those clauses. An unsupported clause previously fell through the hydrated-source predicate as `false`. The request then succeeded with no hits, making an unsupported query indistinguishable from a valid filter that matched nothing. A multi-field term clause had a related problem: only the first field was evaluated.

The gateway now validates the complete `post_filter` tree before it looks up the index or contacts Qdrant. Unsupported query types, unknown bool options, non-numeric range bounds, and clauses with more than one field receive the existing structured HTTP 400 compatibility error. A regression calls search with a nonexistent index and unreachable Qdrant URL, then verifies that an unsupported wildcard post-filter still fails specifically as `post_filter.wildcard`; this makes the fail-before-upstream ordering reproducible without external services.

```bash
cargo test post_filter_validation
cargo test invalid_post_filter_fails_before_index_or_qdrant_lookup
cargo test --all-targets --all-features
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
```

This change does not expand the supported filter set or make `post_filter` counts exact. Post-filtering still operates on the bounded candidate window returned by the main query, and date range evaluation remains outside this hydrated-source path. The benefit is narrower: unsupported semantics are reported honestly instead of being converted into plausible but incorrect empty search results.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-07-post-filters-are-not-aggregation-filters.md

# A post-filter is not an aggregation filter

Elasticsearch applies `post_filter` after aggregations. This lets a catalogue page show only one selected brand while its facet and metric aggregations still describe every document matched by the main query. The gateway applied the post-filter to its hydrated candidate hits before computing min, max, filter, and keyed-filter aggregations, so those aggregations described only the visible hits. Server-side terms facets did not have this bug, which made mixed aggregation responses especially misleading.

The search path now preserves its query-matched candidate window before applying hit-only transformations. Gateway-computed aggregations read that preserved window, while `post_filter`, collapse, and `search_after` continue to affect the returned hits. A request-level regression supplies three products, post-filters hits to the single Acme product, and verifies that a min aggregation still sees the lower-priced Beta products and that a Beta filter aggregation still counts both of them.

```bash
cargo test post_filter_does_not_narrow_gateway_computed_aggregations
cargo test
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
```

This is a semantic correction, not an exact-aggregation implementation. These gateway-computed aggregations still see only the bounded candidate window retrieved for the search, so large or highly selective result sets can remain incomplete. Preserving the pre-filter window also temporarily keeps a second copy of those in-memory candidate values for requests that contain aggregations. Terms aggregations continue to use Qdrant's facet API and do not need that copy.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-06-keyword-multifields-need-one-route.md

# Keyword multi-fields need one route

Elasticsearch clients and application code commonly address an exact-value view as `brand.keyword`. The gateway already treated that conventional suffix as the base `brand` field when it evaluated hydrated source, sorted results, collapsed groups, or requested a terms facet. Native Qdrant filters did not: a `term`, `terms`, `range`, or `exists` clause was sent upstream with the dotted key unchanged. With a base keyword payload, that request searched a field that was never written and could quietly return no hits.

The filter translator and gateway-side pattern collector now use the same suffix normalization as the existing source paths. The focused regression covers all four native predicate shapes, confirms that source evaluation agrees, and exercises a `prefix` query against `sku.keyword`.

Reproduce it with:

```bash
cargo test keyword_multifield_aliases_use_the_base_payload_field
cargo test gateway_patterns_match_keyword_values
```

This is a compatibility alias, not full Elasticsearch multi-field emulation. It does not create a second analyzed value, support custom analyzers, or make an arbitrary text field safe for exact filtering. The base field must already be mapped and mirrored as a filterable payload for native filters to work.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-06-a-page-is-not-a-total.md

# A page is not a total

The gateway used to retrieve at most `from + size` filter matches and then report the length of that candidate window as an exact Elasticsearch `hits.total`. A request for zero hits could therefore say that zero documents matched even when the collection contained many matches. Pagination made the same error less obvious: a ten-hit page could claim the total was ten.

Filter-only searches now reuse the exact Qdrant count operation already used by the `_count` endpoint. A regression fixture exposes 37 matching documents while the search asks for `size: 0`; the gateway sends `{"exact":true}` to Qdrant, keeps the internal scroll limit at one, returns no hit documents, and reports `{"value":37,"relation":"eq"}`. This verifies the protocol behavior without pretending that a local mock is a latency benchmark.

A live check against the repository's pinned Qdrant 1.15.5 image indexed three documents, two with the requested keyword, and returned an exact total of two with an empty hit page. The check waited one second after the bulk write: an immediate probe observed the project's existing refresh approximation and returned zero before the write became visible. That timing is a separate limitation, not evidence that the count path is inaccurate once the write is visible.

```bash
cargo test zero_size_search_uses_a_positive_qdrant_scroll_limit
cargo test --all-targets --all-features
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
```

The accuracy has a cost: an eligible filter-only search now makes a count request as well as its hit-retrieval request. Text searches and searches with `post_filter` still use a bounded candidate window; they now return `relation: "gte"` instead of incorrectly describing that lower bound as exact. Approximate-text and pattern paths already scan all candidates and remain exact. The gateway does not yet implement Elasticsearch's configurable `track_total_hits` threshold, and gateway-computed metric/filter aggregations remain bounded.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-05-sort-shapes-must-not-change-the-order.md

# Sort syntax must not change the order

[Elasticsearch's sort reference](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/sort-search-results) permits a basic field sort as `"price"`, `{"price":"asc"}`, or `{"price":{"order":"desc"}}`. The gateway previously understood only the direct-order object. It treated the standard options object as ascending regardless of its `order`, while a string field silently became `_score` descending. The same misread specification was then used to generate and consume `search_after` values.

Sort clauses now pass through one validated parser before any Qdrant request. Field names default to ascending, `_score` defaults to descending, and both direct and options-object `asc`/`desc` forms drive response ordering, returned sort values, and cursor comparison. `_id` and `_score` are read from hit metadata rather than incorrectly looked up in `_source`. Unsupported options and invalid directions return a structured 400 instead of producing a plausible but wrong page.

The regression uses a three-document response with a price tie. It verifies descending price with `_id` as a tie-breaker, advances past a two-value `search_after` cursor, and checks the single-string ascending form. Reproduce it without a live Qdrant instance:

```bash
cargo test elasticsearch_sort_shapes_drive_order_and_search_after
```

This does not turn response sorting into Qdrant-native global ordering. The gateway still sorts only the bounded candidate window it retrieves, and the cursor remains stable only while that ordered set is unchanged. Large collections or deep ordered pagination should use a native Qdrant ordering design rather than treating this compatibility layer as a distributed sort engine.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-05-arrays-are-multi-valued-fields.md

# Arrays are multi-valued fields, not scalar mismatches

Elasticsearch does not need a separate array field type: an ordinary field can carry several values, and a document matches when an applicable value satisfies the query. Qdrant payload filters use the same practical rule—an array filter succeeds when at least one value meets the condition ([Qdrant payload documentation](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/payload/)).

The gateway already inherited that behavior for filters executed inside Qdrant. Its local source evaluator did not. That evaluator is used by `post_filter`, filter aggregations, and gateway-side `prefix`, `wildcard`, and `regexp` queries. It compared the complete JSON array with one scalar term, required ranges to contain a scalar number, and required pattern fields to be scalar strings. The same document could therefore match a native filter but disappear when the equivalent clause moved to `post_filter`.

The source evaluator now recursively tests scalar values inside arrays and succeeds when any value matches. One regression covers exact term, terms-set, numeric range, prefix, wildcard, and regular-expression predicates over three array-valued fields. It also checks a non-matching range so the rule does not turn into an unconditional array match.

Reproduce the focused check with:

```bash
cargo test gateway_predicates_treat_arrays_as_multi_valued_fields
```

The full Rust suite contains 45 passing unit tests; the live Compose smoke remains opt-in. This change does not add Elasticsearch `nested` query semantics for arrays of objects, and it does not change the gateway's documented response-level sorting or collapse approximations. It only aligns scalar-array predicate evaluation across the native and hydrated-source paths.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-04-optional-should-really-is-optional.md

# Optional should really is optional

Elasticsearch changes the default for `minimum_should_match` according to the other clauses in the same `bool`. A `should`-only query requires one match, but `should` becomes optional when `must` or `filter` is present. The [Elasticsearch bool query reference](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/query-dsl-bool-query.html) documents the defaults as one and zero respectively.

The gateway used to reject the common required-plus-optional shape unless the client explicitly sent `minimum_should_match`. Its gateway-side source evaluator also required one `should` match, which could incorrectly remove hits from `post_filter`, filter aggregations, and approximate lexical scans.

The default is now resolved once and shared by both the Qdrant filter translator and the source evaluator. This regression covers a document that matches `filter.brand = Acme` but not `should.featured = true`: it remains a hit when the minimum is omitted and is excluded when the client explicitly requests one match. A second regression covers the same boundary in the approximate text evaluator.

Run the focused checks without Qdrant:

```bash
cargo test bool_should
```

This aligns hit selection, not scoring. Elasticsearch uses optional query-context clauses to boost relevant documents. Filter-only optional clauses are omitted from the Qdrant filter when their effective minimum is zero, so they do not change Qdrant scores. Clients that require a `should` clause to affect eligibility should continue to send an explicit `minimum_should_match`.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-04-nested-negation-keeps-its-boundary.md

# Nested negation keeps its boundary

Elasticsearch bool clauses accept either one query object or an array. They also preserve the nested bool boundary: excluding a bool that requires both `status = deleted` and `tenant = internal` means `NOT (status = deleted AND tenant = internal)`, not `status != deleted AND tenant != internal`.

The gateway previously handled only the array form of `must_not`. A scalar negative clause was silently omitted. When a nested bool appeared inside `must_not` or `should`, its inner `must_not` clauses were also discarded, and multiple required conditions under one negation were flattened into separate exclusions. Those cases widened or narrowed the result set without warning.

The Qdrant filter translator now builds one explicit filter condition for each nested clause. Required and excluded children stay grouped before the parent applies negation or `min_should`. The regression covers scalar double negation, a negative bool inside `should`, and the distinction between `NOT (A AND B)` and `NOT A AND NOT B`.

Run the focused check without Qdrant:

```bash
cargo test bool_negative_clauses_preserve_scalar_and_nested_semantics
```

The emitted shapes were also exercised against the pinned Qdrant 1.15.5 image. With one `deleted` and one `live` point, double negation selected only `deleted`; the negative `should` alternative selected only `live`.

This correction covers filter-only term, terms, range, exists, IDs, and nested bool conditions. Text queries under `must_not` or filter-only `should` remain rejected because translating their scoring and exclusion semantics safely requires a different execution path.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-03-pattern-counts-must-scan-source.md

# Pattern counts must scan the source

The gateway evaluates `wildcard`, `prefix`, and `regexp` clauses against hydrated `_source` documents because Qdrant does not receive an equivalent native filter. Search already followed that rule, but `_count` did not: it removed the pattern while building the Qdrant filter and then called Qdrant's count endpoint. A pattern-only count therefore returned the size of the whole collection.

Pattern counts now use the same paginated source scan and matching rules as pattern searches. A regression serves two mock Qdrant scroll pages containing `ABC-100`, `XYZ-100`, and `ABC-200`; `{"wildcard":{"sku":"ABC-*"}}` returns `2` and makes two scroll requests instead of an unfiltered count request.

Run the focused check without a Qdrant process:

```bash
cargo test count_applies_gateway_patterns_across_scroll_pages
```

This improves correctness, not query cost. A pattern-only count is linear in the candidate set, retains matching hits while the shared search path computes its total, and can observe concurrent writes between scroll pages. It is appropriate for modest catalog fields; large or latency-sensitive deployments should model a natively indexed exact-match field instead.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-03-manufacturing-maintenance-queue.md

# The pump is fixed. Take it off the queue.

A maintenance planner at a Leeds factory needs open pump faults, not last week's completed inspections or another plant's backlog. These five synthetic work orders make that distinction testable. Closing a job should remove it from the queue while preserving its original notes.

Use a running Elasticsearch-compatible endpoint and a fresh `field_note_maintenance` index. The client below is curl: run the same commands for each server, changing only `ES` (`http://localhost:19200` for Elasticsearch or `http://localhost:9200` for the gateway).

```sh
ES=http://localhost:19200
curl -fsS -X PUT "$ES/field_note_maintenance" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"mappings":{"properties":{"title":{"type":"text"},"plant":{"type":"keyword"},"team":{"type":"keyword"},"status":{"type":"keyword"},"downtime_minutes":{"type":"integer"}}}}'

curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_maintenance/_bulk?refresh=wait_for" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-ndjson' --data-binary @- <<'NDJSON'
{"index":{"_id":"wo-101"}}
{"title":"Pump seal leaking","plant":"Leeds","team":"mechanical","status":"open","downtime_minutes":45}
{"index":{"_id":"wo-102"}}
{"title":"Conveyor belt slipping","plant":"Leeds","team":"mechanical","status":"open","downtime_minutes":20}
{"index":{"_id":"wo-103"}}
{"title":"Pump motor overheating","plant":"Bristol","team":"electrical","status":"open","downtime_minutes":60}
{"index":{"_id":"wo-104"}}
{"title":"Pump inspection complete","plant":"Leeds","team":"mechanical","status":"closed","downtime_minutes":0}
{"index":{"_id":"wo-105"}}
{"title":"Sensor signal intermittent","plant":"Leeds","team":"electrical","status":"open","downtime_minutes":10}
NDJSON
sleep 5
```

The five-second pause is the same on both endpoints; this check does not establish immediate search visibility after a gateway refresh.

Find open pump jobs at Leeds:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_maintenance/_search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"size":10,"query":{"bool":{"must":{"match":{"title":"pump"}},"filter":[{"term":{"plant":"Leeds"}},{"term":{"status":"open"}}]}}}'
```

Only `wo-101`, “Pump seal leaking”, should return, with its complete source. The Bristol pump fault and the completed Leeds inspection must stay out.

Count all open Leeds jobs by team, independently of the pump text search:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_maintenance/_search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"size":0,"query":{"bool":{"filter":[{"term":{"plant":"Leeds"}},{"term":{"status":"open"}}]}},"aggs":{"teams":{"terms":{"field":"team","size":10}}}}'
```

Expect `mechanical: 2` and `electrical: 1`, with no hits because `size` is zero. Now close the leaking-pump job and read it back:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_maintenance/_update/wo-101?refresh=wait_for" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"doc":{"status":"closed"}}'
sleep 5
curl -fsS "$ES/field_note_maintenance/_doc/wo-101"
```

The update returns `updated`; the read retains the title, plant, team, and 45 minutes of downtime, with `status: closed`. Repeat the two search requests: the pump result is empty and both team buckets are now `1`. The history survives; the actionable queue shrinks.

The [deterministic replay](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/manufacturing.py) checks these requests against explicit expectations on each server, including every document's ID and source. The [recorded run](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/manufacturing-2026-10-03.json) used Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and gateway 0.1.3 backed by Qdrant 1.15.3; all 62 checks passed with identical application requests and no gateway code change. This is a five-document correctness check, with no performance claim.

Boundary: Lucene score equivalence, refresh timing guarantees, and atomic concurrent updates are outside this example's [supported semantics](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/compatibility/).

To remove only this example's index afterward:

```sh
curl -fsS -X DELETE "$ES/field_note_maintenance"
```


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-03-exists-means-not-empty.md

# Exists means not empty

The gateway translated an Elasticsearch `exists` query directly into Qdrant's `is_empty` condition. That is the opposite predicate: documents with a missing, `null`, or empty-array value were selected, while documents with a real value were excluded.

The translation now negates `is_empty`. The same definition is used when the gateway evaluates a `post_filter` against hydrated `_source`: missing values, `null`, `[]`, and `[null]` do not exist; `""` and `[null, "Acme"]` do.

An isolated check against the repository's pinned Qdrant 1.15.3 image inserted those five boundary cases. The emitted filter returned only point 4 (the empty string) and point 5 (the array containing `"Acme"`):

```json
{"filter":{"must":[{"must_not":[{"is_empty":{"key":"brand"}}]}]}}
```

The regression checks are reproducible without a running Qdrant instance:

```bash
cargo test exists_query_excludes_empty_qdrant_payloads
cargo test post_filter_exists_rejects_missing_null_and_empty_arrays
```

This is not a claim of complete Elasticsearch field-existence parity. Server-side filtering applies to mapped fields mirrored into the searchable Qdrant payload, and the gateway does not emulate mapping-dependent cases such as `index: false`, `ignore_above`, or malformed values ignored during indexing.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-02-zero-results-still-need-a-positive-scroll.md

# Zero results still need a positive scroll

Elasticsearch clients commonly send `"size": 0` when they need aggregations but no document hits. The gateway passed that value through as Qdrant's scroll `limit`, turning a valid search into an upstream error.

An isolated check against the Qdrant 1.15.3 image pinned by this repository made the incompatibility concrete: the same empty collection returned HTTP 422 for `{"limit":0}` with `must be 1 or larger`, and HTTP 200 for `{"limit":1}`. The gateway now floors only the internal scroll limit at one, then applies the requested zero-sized page when it builds the Elasticsearch response. A regression test verifies both sides of that boundary: Qdrant receives `limit: 1`, while the client receives an empty `hits.hits` array.

```bash
cargo test zero_size_search_uses_a_positive_qdrant_scroll_limit
cargo test --all-targets --all-features
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
```

This removes the 502 failure and lets server-side terms facets run for aggregation-only searches. It does not make all aggregation and total-count behavior exact: search totals and gateway-computed metric/filter aggregations are still bounded by the candidate window described in the compatibility guide.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-02-mapping-updates-must-not-erase-the-map.md

# Mapping updates must not erase the map

Elasticsearch sends a mapping update as `{"properties": ...}`, while index creation nests the same object under `mappings`. The gateway reused the index-creation parser for both shapes. A normal `PUT /products/_mapping` therefore interpreted the update as an empty mapping and replaced the stored definition with `{}`, silently losing the fields used to build search vectors and filter payloads for later writes.

Mapping updates now merge properties under the same index-administration lock used by other catalogue changes. Supported keyword, boolean, integer, float, and date additions also create the corresponding Qdrant payload index before the merged mapping is published in SQLite. Repeating an identical field definition is a no-op; changing an existing definition returns a structured 400 instead of rewriting search behavior.

The regression starts with a `title` text mapping, adds a `brand` keyword property using the Elasticsearch request shape, and verifies all three boundaries: `title` remains stored, `brand` gets a Qdrant keyword index, and the existing sparse-vector list is unchanged.

```bash
cargo test mapping_updates_merge_properties_and_create_payload_indexes
cargo test --all-targets --all-features
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
```

An isolated check against the repository's pinned Qdrant 1.15.3 image confirmed that the emitted payload-index request creates `payload_schema.brand` as `keyword`. This does not make every Elasticsearch mapping mutation available. In particular, new text fields are rejected because that Qdrant version cannot add the required named sparse vector to an existing collection; create a new index and reindex when the searchable text schema changes. If a multi-field payload-index update fails partway through, Qdrant may retain an unused index, but the gateway does not publish the partial mapping.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-01-invalid-utf8-is-not-source-data.md

# Invalid UTF-8 is not source data

The gateway used to convert every HTTP body with a lossy UTF-8 decoder before parsing JSON or bulk NDJSON. An invalid byte inside a quoted value therefore became the Unicode replacement character (`U+FFFD`). If the value was source data or a bulk `_id`, the request could remain syntactically valid and write data under a value the client never sent.

The HTTP boundary now requires strict UTF-8 and returns a structured HTTP 400 response with `feature: request.body` before endpoint dispatch. The same check covers ordinary JSON, bulk, and multi-search requests. It runs after the configured byte limit, so oversized bodies still receive the more useful HTTP 413 response without an additional allocation beyond the already bounded body.

The regression injects byte `0xff` into a quoted document field and a quoted bulk identifier, then verifies that both requests are rejected with the Elasticsearch product header:

```bash
cargo test invalid_utf8_request_bodies_are_rejected_without_lossy_replacement
cargo test --all-targets --all-features
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
```

This validation does not normalize valid Unicode or require ASCII. UTF-8 document content and identifiers continue to work unchanged, while clients that produce malformed encodings must correct or explicitly transcode them before sending JSON.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-01-alias-batches-are-one-routing-change.md

# Alias batches are one routing change

Elasticsearch's aliases API accepts a list of actions so clients can express a routing change as one request. The gateway previously applied each action to its SQLite catalogue while it was still parsing later actions. A valid `add` followed by a malformed `remove` could therefore return HTTP 400 after the new alias was already visible.

The gateway now validates every action first. Each item must contain exactly one supported `add` or `remove` action with object metadata and string `index` and `alias` values. Only after all target indices and alias-name conflicts have passed validation does one SQLite transaction apply the complete list. Removal also matches both alias and concrete index, rather than deleting an alias that points somewhere else.

The regression first submits a valid add followed by a remove with no index and verifies that no alias was added. It then switches an existing alias from `products-v1` to `products-v2` with a two-action request and verifies the committed target:

```sh
cargo test alias_actions_validate_before_an_atomic_catalogue_update
```

This guarantee covers the gateway's local metadata catalogue. The current alias model still has one target per alias; it does not implement filtered aliases, multi-index fan-out, write-index selection, wildcard actions, or a distributed transaction with Qdrant. Deployments with independent SQLite catalogues must still coordinate alias changes outside the gateway.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-09-30-bulk-mutations-need-document-ids.md

# Bulk mutations need document IDs

Elasticsearch requires bulk `update` and `delete` actions to identify the document they mutate. The gateway previously generated a random ID whenever `_id` was absent. That was particularly misleading for deletes: a malformed request could report `not_found` for a generated ID even though the caller never selected a document.

The bulk parser now returns a structured HTTP 400 before executing any item when an `update` or `delete` action omits `_id`. This preflight behavior also prevents earlier valid items in the same request from being applied before the malformed action is discovered. `index` and `create` retain their existing generated-ID behavior.

The same change accepts both `POST` and `PUT` for root and index-scoped `_bulk` routes, matching the documented Elasticsearch API surface. Regression tests exercise both missing-ID action types and verify that PUT requests receive the dedicated bulk body limit.

This does not add optimistic concurrency control: bulk sequence-number, primary-term, and version semantics remain outside the current compatibility subset.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-09-30-bulk-action-metadata-is-a-write-boundary.md

# Bulk action metadata is a write boundary

A bulk action line decides which operation, index, and document ID the gateway will mutate. Treating malformed metadata as if it were absent is therefore unsafe: a numeric `_id`, for example, previously fell through to generated-ID behavior for `index` and `create` actions. An action line containing more than one operation also silently selected whichever key the JSON object exposed first.

The gateway now validates the complete bulk request before executing any item.
